div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

It "a friend in need is a friend indeed," why are we not glad to see a poor relation? MR. COBB' has married Miss Webb. He knew that they were meant to be joined as soon as he ez)eil her. MARIANNA, whom Tennyson describes as "gazing athwart toe gloomy fiats,' was probably engaged is house hunting. ENGLAN u's puzzle and Pat's charade—" You roue MN first by asking rent for my second, and my whole is my country ' —lreland. VViir is praising children like opium? Because it is lawiing 'em (laudanum). FALLING DUE. —" Bleed is the man," said kins, in the late dry weather, " whose bills are falling due (dew). "Tonv, what did the Isrs elites do when they crossed the Red Sea ?" "I (Junin); but I gueth they dried themselves." " WHY, Hans, you have the most feminine cast of countenance I have ever z•een." " Oh, yali replied Hans; "the reason oi dat is because my mother WA S a voomans." "On !" exclaimed a pretentious writer, " what a pain there is in my head !" "Do you complain of that r said a friend ; "you ought to be thank- ful that there is anything in it." THE eternal fitness of things was maintained by the young roan who recently- went to his own wedding and his father'a funeral on the same day, wearing white at his wedding and black at the funeral. "Ifs a good thing to have a handsome penman for a beau, ' said Mary, as she glanced over a billet- doux. " Yes," replied Julia ; "if the penman is only handsome, I don't care how homely the pen- manship is." ins following was posted up in the county of Bent in the year 1821 :—" Notice is hereby given that the Marquis of Camden (on account of the backwardness of the harvest) will not shoot him- self or any of his tenants till the 14th of Sep- tember." AUGUSTUS was manipulating the lawnmower in the evening, by way of exercise, and his wife sat on the piazza watching him. "Why is Augustus like one that is deceased ?" she asked her sister, who could not tell. "Because he is no mower." And now there is grief in the household. A PLASTERER and his boy being employed to whitewash a house by the day were so tedious that owner asked the lad in his master's absence when he thought they would have done. The boy bluntly replied, " Master's looking for another job, and if he finds one, we shall finish this week." LITTLE Marm--" Mamma, where do people go when they die ?" Mamma—" Oh, you must not ask such questions, dear; you will understand all about it when you are a little older." Little Maud (after some reflection)—" Mamma, do you know all about it ?" " Aw, my good man, what kind of a wesidence do you think would suit me?" asked an exquisite of a house agent. After taking him in, eye-glass and all, the ageat replied: "Something like a fiat, I should think, would be most appropriate." A JUVENILE, on coming home for a vacation, astounded his father by asking, "Why's my education like iced hock and seltzer?" And before the amazed father could reply, the young rogue added, "Because it's schooling (it's cooling). ' A NUMBER of ladies were chatting about their dislike of the use of tobacco by their husbands, • when one of them declared, "1 never kiss my husband because he smokes !" and then amid the general silence she added; "No, I kiss him because .I. like to." We lately read of a person who was killed by a cork, which struck him in the eye when drawing it. But if the cork has killed its one man, consider how many thousands and tens of thousands the bottle has killed, without a word being.said about it.

A FEENCH JOKE.—" Do you know Mlle.X?" " Yes, she's a charming little thing." "Only she doequ't talk much." "flow can she help it?" " What ! Isn't she clever?" " Yes, but she won't say anything bad about anybody—that's why she is so silent.' THE young man, says the Marathon (N.Y.) Inde- pendent, who sent us by mail a manuscript poem beginning, " 'Twas night bet ore Christmas," claim- ing it to be original, will understand that all we -could find original about it was the spelling. Henceforth we meet as trangers. A MAN having been arraigned for ill-treating his wife, the Justice took him roundly to task for "beating his wife in the public street !" "1 see, your honour," said the culprit," where my mistake was. Hereafter I'll beat her in private, as your honour's remarks suggest." A GENTLEMAN in New Orleans was agreeably surprised the other day to find a plump turkey served up for dinner, and inquired of his servant how it was obtained. "Why, sir," replied Sambo, " dat turkey has been roosting on our fence tree nights, so dis morning I seize him for de rent of de fence." AL TALIATRASD was enjoying his rubber, when the conversation turned on the recent union of an
elderly lady of respectable rank. "However could Madame_ de S— make such a match? A

person of her birth to marry a valet-de-ohambre Ah," replied Talleyrand, "it was late in the game. At nine we don't reckon honours." ETILZLBERTA—" I want a pair of slippers for pa. Number tens, please, and—squeaky." Genial shoemaker—" Squeaky, Mies? I'm afraid we haven't any of that kind." Ethelberta—" lam so
sorry. COuldn't you make him a squeaky pair? There is a certain young gentleman who visits me frequently, and—and it would be very convenient for him to know just when pa is coining home."

Tax following story about one of the members for Leicester is worth repeating. The other night this gentleman appeared, for the first time, in the House in evening dress. The apparition excited amazement, and a young Conservative whispered to one of the occupants of the Treasury bench, "Picton's been out to preach." "No," was the prompt answer of the Minister, "he has not; he's hired a snit, and comes here to wait." And, as • matter of fact, he did wait until four o'clock in the morning. THE nobler sex "can't be bothered" with minutice. "What is a paltry five pound to me?" I have heard said in excuse of its quite unnecessary expenditure "when every day I have to deal with hundreds and thousands." Or, "Why keep daily accounts? My clerks do that. For me, I just put two or three pounds in my pocket, spend them till they are gone—and then put in two or three more." I appeal to the candid masculine mind if this is not the ordinary way of thinking at least of those to whom Fate has kindly given the "two or three pounds" always in pocket, without need to beg, borrow, or steal ?—Mrs. Craik. THE MOST POPULAR. MAN Or TIIE AGE.—After old Governor Bouck's retirement from office, a number of unlettered admirers in Rennsalaer county held an "admiration meeting" in his honour. The person employed to write out the leading toast for the occasion, being an irrestrain- able wag, handed the dull-witted presiding officer the following, which he read with great unction, and which the meeting received with enthusiastic cheers: "Ex-Governer William C. Bouck, the most popular man of the age: He went in with very little opposition, and went out with no oppo- sition at all 1' AN &Kamm:TAN once expressed great surprise in a company of /iterati at Edinburgh, that the Scotch should be so much addicted to smuggling, seeing that they are a remarkably sober and moral people. He thought it must be much against their conscience. "Oh, not at all, sir," said Mr. a noted punster, who was present ; "what is conscience, but a entail gill voice ?" " Farther," added Professor W—, "1t is the worm that never dies."

PASSAGES of Scripture, like Acts of Parliament, are sometimes curiously interpreted. A young lady was seen by her. father one day to kiss a young man. He severely rebuked her, and asked, "Have I not always instructed you to follow the teachings of your Bible?" The young lady answered that her conduct was allowed, and even commanded in the Bible in the following passage: —" Whatsoever ye would that men should do unto you do ye even so to them." Ax Irishman, who lives with a Grahamite, writes to a friend that, if he wants to know what "litigant living" be, be must come te. his house, where the breakfast consists oi uo.,iii,g, ~,d the supper of what was left at breakfast.

Madame Jlelba has an iTiterest in the Kanaka question to the extent of one thousand two hundred and eighty acres near Mackey, one of the chief centres of the Queensland sugar-growing industry. Her solicitors have commenced proceedings with the object of having this land vested in her own name under the provisions of the recently-adopted Queensland Married Women's Property Act. Cap- tain Armstrong, Madame Melba's husband, and the petitioner for a divorce, was for some time the manager of a sugar-growing estate in the same district.

Lady Mary Vyner, whose death is recorded at the ripe age of eighty-three, was the daughter of Lord Grantham, afterwards the first Lord de Grey. As Lady Mary Robinson, which was the family name, she was celebrated for her extreme beauty, and more than one octogenarian still lives who re- members the flutter of expectation in St. James's Church, Piccadilly. when the rustle of her dainty skirts was heard. She was noted for her personal acts of charity and kindness at a period when they were rare among the cultured classes, he mar- ried a Mr. Thomas Vyner, whom she survived.

The Countess of Munster, who has recently pub-, lished another novel, entitled " The Scotch Earl,' is one of the most successful of literary ladies of title. And she does not hesitate to admit that she writes for money, and not for "the love of the thing." Lord Monster, though the grandson of King William IV., is himself not a wealthy man. One of their sons, the Hon. Aubrey Fitzclarence, held for a considerable time a city clerkship at a ridiculously small wage; but the Queen greatly distressed at seeing the great grandson oi an Eng• lish monarch ekeing out a scanty subsistence, ap- pointed him to a place at court. He is now what is called a" quarterly usher" in-waiting.

There has been but one double return to the new Parliament. 31r. William O'Brien has been elected for the city of Cork and for one of the divisions of Cork county. Several gentlemen have however stood for more than one constituency. Mr. Justin M'Carthy, defeated in Derry, has been elected for Longford; Mr. Sexton, defeated in Belfast, has found a seat in Kerry; Mr. Sullivan, defeated in Dublin, has been returned for West Donegal; Mr. W. Redmond, defeated in Cork City, is member for East Clare; and Mr. Alexander Blane has been de- feated both in Armagh and West Meath.

Wesleyan Methodists will have two of their most prominent members in the new House of Commons in Alderman W. H. Holland, of Salford, and Mr. W. 0. Clough,one of the Liberal victors in Portsmsuth. Alderman Holland, who checked the career of Mr. Baumann on Wednesday has lived all his life in Salford, where he is now a wealthy manufacturer and large enployer of labour. He is himself a skilled mechanic, and the happiest relations exist' between him and his wock-people. Alderman Holland is a handsome, solid-looking man, who has filled many offices in connection with the Wesleyan body in Salford.

—A correspondent writes to the "Star :"—You are not quite accurate as to the number of Roman Catholics who will sit in the new Parliament for English and Scotch constituencies. You give four as the number, and mention Sir Charles Russell, Mr. J. Austin, Mr. Henry Matthews, and Mr. MacFarlane. The number is, however, six, the other two being Mr. T. P. O'Connor, for the Scotland Division of Liverpool, and Mr. W.Smith, for the North Lonsdale Division of Lancashire. Mr. Smith is a new qcces- Mon to the Liberal ranks, and enters Parliament with the distinction of having wrested his seat from a Unionist. He has been Mayor of Lancaster.

The delight with which the defeat of Lord Cranborne has been hailed by the Radical party is explained by the fact that his lordship's demeanour has long been to them a subject of just resentment. Lord Cranborne, who is thirty-one, and looks con- siderably younger, readily caught the tone of his father, and in the early days of the late Parliament signalised himself by rude interruptions when Mr. Gladstone was speaking. On one of these occasions Mr. Healy looked at him from the opposite side of the /louse, and created a burst of unrestrained merriment by the remark, " Quiet,young Salisbury; quiet, boy."

similarly the defeat of Viscount Weymouth, the eldest son of the Marquis of Batli,and the late Tory member for the Frome Division of Somersetshire, has created great rejoicing in the West. Lord Weymouth, like Sir John Colomb, who has been ejected from Bow, got into Parliament by pledging himself to Tote against Coercion. Mr. Sexton dur- ing the debate on the Coercion Bill in 1887,held up in his place in the House of Commons a placard which had been posted on every dead wall in the Frome division with the words "Vote for Wey- mouth and no Coercion" in large capitals. Mr. Sexton's appeal to the noble lord to stand by his pledge was answered by an insolent guffaw from the Tory benches. The eminently satisfactory result of the Dunlo marriage—we refer, of course, to the period subse- quent to the time when an angry father tempted an unwilling son to failure in the Divorce Court—has encouraged the head of the house of Fitzmaurice (the Orkney Fitzmaurices) to imitation and pos- sibly emulation. Miss Connie Gilchrist, the pet alike of stalls and gallery, of peer and poet, is now Countess of Orkney. As a child she wore straw- berry leaves woven in her luxuriant tresses. As a woman her locks are surmounted by a coronet. " He felt sure that by marrying Lady Orkney he had accomplished the best day's work he had ever done in his life.' So spake the Earl at the wedding feast

llolker Hall, in Lancashire, which will be the bridal residence of Mr. Victor Cavendish, LP., was always the favourate residence of the late Duke of Devonshire, though Chatsworth is undoubtedly the most magnificent of the country palaces of the House of Cavendish. It was here that the last years of the life of the late Duke were spent when he had become too feeble to undertake the fatigue of trav- elling. The house is an antique structure in good preservation, which dates backs to the reign of glizabeth, when it belonged to the Preston family. From them it passed to the Lowthers, and came to its present owner by marriage. It is situated on the left bank of the estuary of the Leven, and is surrounded by noble woods.

It is an open secret that on his retirement from office in 1886 and again in 1887, on the occasion of the Jubilee, her Majesty offered Lord Salisbury a dukedom. The Prime Minister declined the honour; but it is thought probable that it will again be pressed upon him by the Queen at the expiration of his second Administration, and that this time it will not be refused. The Marquisate of Salisbury is only a little more than a century old, having been conferred on the seventh earl in 1789. The first Marquis by the way resembled his successor in his love of science, and had the honour of being elected a Fellow of the Royal Society, besides being well-known in the political world. The Earldom of Salisbury dates from 1605, when it was conferred by James I. on the famous statesman, Robert Cecil, second son of the even more illustrious Lord Burghley. Another duke is likely to be created by the elevation of the Marquis of Lansdowne, on the expiration of his term of office in India, to the Dukedom of Kerry.

We do not suppose that Mr. Leonard Courtney will be called upon to preside over the new House in Committee. But whoever the next chairman may be he will be interested in a decision just pro- nounced by the Supreme Court of New South Wales. During a stormy all night sitting of the Legislative Assembly at Sydney, Mr. J. M. Toohey, an Irish- Australian brewer, and one of the members for Sydney, was pronounced to be persistently disor- ' derly by the chairman, who eventually ordered his removal from the Chamber. The Serjeant-at-Arms obeyed the order, and Mr. Toohey then brought an action against the chairman, claiming £2,000 damages on the ground that a member cannot be removed from the Chamber without a previous re- solution of the House to that effect. The full court of the colony has decided that there is no legal force in 3.1 r. Toohey's contention, and that the chairman yi vested with power and authority to order of his own accord the removal of a disorderly member from the Chamber. Mr. Toohey is not yet satisfied, and threatens to appeal to the Privy Council.

Lovers of Robert Burns's poems will regret to hear that a great grandson of the Ayrshire poet, a Mr. Robert Burns Hutchinson, is at present living in sad circumstances at Chicago. He has been struggling for some time against adverse fortune and bad health to secure a livelihood for himself, his wife, and infant son, when, on the 7th of last

month, on his way home from business, he was attacked by footpads, robbed of his watch, money, and some of his clothes, severely handled, thrown into a hole, and left for dead. After lying uncon- scious for some hours he managed to drag himself to his home only to become insensible from loss of blood. The injuries he received are very serious, he has not yet recovered consciousness, and his survival up to now has greatly surprised his medi- cal attendants. Should he live it will be a long time before he is able to do anything towards the support of his wife and son, who are now unfortu- nately dependent upon the charity of friends. Mr. John Muir, of 48, Abbotsford-place, Glasgow, editor of a publication called the " Annual Burns Chronicle," has opened a subscription in aid of this last surviving male descendant of the poet.

div.head: WARRINGTON CORPORATION ACCOUNTS. A YEAR'S FINANCE.
div.p: WARRINGTON CORPORATION ACCOUNTS. A YEAR'S FINANCE.

Toe report in which Mr. Chorley, the Warrington. borough treasurer, sets out the receipts and expen- diture of the Corporation for the year beginning March 26th, 1891, and ending March 25th, 1892, is a bulky volume of some 248 pages. There is no literary lightness about it; it is in fact a printed ledger with receipts on one side and expenditure on the other, all the items being set forth under their respective headings as compactly and concisely as possible. First of all we come to the accounts of the

WATCH DEPARTMENT in which the largest item of expenditure is, of course, the police constables' wages which stand at £3,886 178. 11d., to which has to be added the Chief Constable's salary of £3OO. There is £322 13s. 7d. for constables' clothing and boot allowance, and then we have allowance for maintenance of prisoners £64 18s., and of dogs £6 13s. 6d. The police superannuation fund seems to be in a flour- ishing condition as there is only one pensioner—ex- P.C. R. Singleton—upon it. Either Warrington policemen are so long-lived that they disdain to be superannuated, or they are too short-lived to reach the requisite length, or, perhaps, there is. so much " moving on " in the police force that a long-service man is a rarity. Whatever be the reason, there is no doubt about the fact that the police have to contribute 21d. per cent, of their pay towards the superannuation fund and this amounts to a total of .£94 2s. 3d. in the year, with an addi- tional £7 10s. deducted from the Chief Constable's salary. The assets of the fund are £7,300 in Warrington Corporation bonds, £397 3s. 6d. in the hands of the banker, and £215 in "the form of a gas annuity. As might be expected there is nothing lively about the

CEMETERY FINANCE. The chief sources of income ate—for the purchase of graves, .£355 12s. ; excavating, &c., £254 11; and fees charged after first interment £220 12s. On the expenditure side of the sheet there is a sum of £765 15s. paid for interest on and towards the redemption of the debt on the cemetery, registrar's salary and for assistance, .£l3O, and gardeners and labourers wages £230 13s. 6(1. Church burial fees amounted to no less than £199 75., distributed as follows :—The Rector and his clerk, £B4 108. 6d ; vicar of St. Paul's and clerk and sextJn,..£4s 4s. 10d; vicar of St. James, do., £l2 12s. ; vicar of St. Anne's, do., £29 65.; vicar of Holy Trinity, do., £l9 Bs. ; vicar of St. Barnabas, do., £8 ss. Bd. In the accounts of the

The receipts from fair and market tolls, rents of shops in market hall, stalls, &c., amounted to £3,662 2s. 7d., while on the other side of the sheet for wages, and a variety of other incidental expenses, stands, an I expenditure of £1,135 7s. 4d. Next we come to the famous LONGFORD MANURE WORKS AND INTERCEPTING DEPOTS which are supposed to be the profit-making department of the Sanitary Committee's work. div.head: STRANGE STORY.
div.p: A STRANGE STORY.

An American soldier tells the following strange story of the Civil War:—" We had crossed the river to hunt for Lee and give him battle in the Wilder- ness. Darkness was settling down, and the advance had halted for the night, when a squad of cavalry brought in a young man from our front. He wore a mixed uniform, as did most of the Confederates at that day, or as did most of those belonging to the partisan commands. He had on blue trousers, a butternut jacket, and his hat belonged to neither side. They said he was a spy. They said it care- lessly enough, but there was an awful significance in the term at that hour. In camp he would have been searched, interrogated, and imprisoned. It might have been weeks before his trial, and he would be allowed every chance for life.

"We were on the mare. There had been fight- ing. There would be more to-morrow. That meant a drumhead trial for the spv. "how speedily everything was arranged! I was at headquarters, and saw and heard it all. Within half an hour a court-martial was convened—grave- faced officers who looked into the face of the young man at first with interest—then with something like admiration.

"I said a young man. I was wrong. He was a boy of seventeen or eighteen. He had big blue eyes, chestnut curls, and his cheek was as smooth as a girl's. He was a handsome lad, and I believe that every man in the tent felt pity for him. " What's your name?' "' James Blank.' '"What regiment?' "No reply. " 'Are you a citizen or soldier?' "No reply. " Can you make any defence to the charge of being a spy?' "No reply. "The officers looked at each other ani nodded, and the president waved his hand. It didn't seem a minute before a file of soldiers came, The face of the boy grew white, but he moved like one in a dream. His big blue eyes looked upon one after another, as if searching for a friend, and my heart yearned to cry out that he was only a boy and ought to be given time. "Tramp! tramp! tramp! "It was the detail marching him off into the darkness.

" Halt! Tie this handkerchief over his eyes!' " They had brought a lantern. By its light I new the big blue eyes for the last time as they looked around in a dazed way. I wanted to shout to the boy and warn him that it was not even yet too late to,prove that he was not what they thought him to be, but the grinmess of the scene paralysed ray tongue. ' " Place him there. Fall back Attention ! Ready—aim—fire!' "Ten minutes later the officer in charge of the firing party touched his cap and reported Orders have been executed, sir!" Any further evidence?' '"No, sir, except that she was a young woman!''
HOW A FAMOUS NOVELIST OBTAINED HIS WIFE.

An official high in the employ of the Government told the following remarkable story to a Kansas newspaper man the other day:— " The story of how Robert Louis Stevenson got his wife ha a never been told in print, I believe. The story sounds almost like a chapter from a novel, but is, nevertheless, absolutely true in all its details. "In 1855, I, a young man, became intimately acquainted, with Samuel C. Osborne, who was then private secretary to Governor Willard, of Indiana. Osborne was a magnificent fellow in personal appearance and magnetism. He was versatile, scholarly, witty, quick as the lightning's flash in repartee, and a fine musician. That man could draw sweeter tones from a flute than any man I ever know. Well,in 1858, Osborne married a black- eyed Miss Vandergrift ; she was not beautiful by any means, but rather attractive. At that time he was in the office of the reporter of the Supreme Court of Indiana, and was making good money. "in 1861 James B. Beach,reporter of the Supreme Court, and Osborne, both of whom had saved up a few thousands of dollars, started for Arizona. Sam had his wife and two children, a boy and a girl, and lie took them along. Arrived in Arizona, Beach and Osborne bought a mine with their savings, and in about a month were offered 100,000d018. in cash for their bonanza. Beach wanted to hold on for a larger offer, and inside of six weeks they could not sell for a dollar. Osborne headed for San Francisco, and reached the Golden Gate with 7dols. in his pocket. He knew a good deal of law, and was a good stenographer, tine of the fastest in the coun- try at that time. This accomplishment stood him in hand, for he was soon making lots of money, and sometimes he used to write to me he would get I,ooodols. for reporting a single case. As years went on the daughter and son grew up and were sent abroad to finish their education. The son went to England and the daughter to France. The mother went to Europe and spent a season or two with them. "The last time Mrs. Osborne went over was in 1883, and then she met Itobert Louis Stevenson—l believe it was in Paris. She at once wrote back to her husband, and told of meeting the literary genius, and told of an affection she had formed for him. Osborne evidently thought this a merely platonic affection, and, I guess, had good reason to think so, for he wrote her that if she loved Steven- son to come back to 'Frisco and obtain a divorce. She did this, and as soon as the divorce was granted the invitations for her marriage to Robert Louis Stevenson were sent out. The bridegroom was in town during the divorce proceedings. Osborne was invited to the wedding, and he accepted. He ap- peared on that evening dressed faultlessly, and having on his arm a lady of rare beauty. The wedding over, the new Mrs. Stevenson introduced her new husband to her former one, and Osborne in turn represented the lady on his arm as Mrs. Samuel C. Osborne! He had been quietly married to her as soon as the divorce was granted. Osborne would make no outward sign, but the episode broke his heart. He went to Australia, and Stevenson to Samoa. I have neve:* heard from Osborne since. The places and men that knew him know him no more, and I do not know whether he is living or •dead."

div.head: [ALL RIERTS RESERVED.]
div.p: [ALL RIERTS RESERVED.]
THE CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS.
BY LILLIAS WASSERMAN, Author of "Some Fisher Folk," "Judith," "Where the North Wind Blows," &e., die.
CuArn LVIL AN APPEAL TO SILVIA.
Lady Callerley knew nothing of her husband's last visit to Breamish HalL

Bitter as Sir Lancelot's anger still burned against the worker of mischief, be could not bring himself to betray a woman's confidence, and that woman his kinswoman. Her frantic passion inspired him with a repugnance little short of loathing, and he felt ashamed even to have listened to her avowal of it.

A conceited man might, indeed, have had his vanity pleasantly tickled with the notion that a fine handsome woman was so madly enamoured of him, but whatever Sir Lancelot's failings might be they did not include coxcombry. Shameful was the passion, and shameful did he feel at having unconsciously inspired it. Therefore the less that was said about it the better for all parties. With no fuel to feed the flame the fire must assuredly die out. He simply told Sylvia that he had found Dorothy Breamish to be a deceitful, double dealing, danger- ous woman; and desired that all communication between Seaton Callerley and Breamish Hall might oease, at any rate for a time. Lady Callerley was only too happy to obey this injunction, and consequently for the past few weeks nothing had been seen or heard either of the Squire or Madam. When the latter entered the cottage it was quite evident that she was not sure of what her greeting might be. Her pale and haggard looks moved Silvia to com- ssion • and she, Lady Callerley, was so supremely happy herself that--she could not endure to think of anyone else being miserable. Sorrow and pain had enlarged her nature, and had endowed her with woman's best gift—sympathy. Then the joy which had come at last and flooded her life with sunshire, made her wishful that all the world shoulu rejoice with her. Would Lancelot be very angry if she spoke, and spoke kindly to this poor, wretched, worn-looking creature? •

No, she was sure he would forgive Mrs. Beamish himself, could he only see her ! Besides, the idea suggested by the Squire during his talk when he was at Seaton Callerley, had stayed in Lady Cal- lerley's mind, and predisposed her to think more pitifully of the culprit. It was Bell who first broke the silence in the cottage; for Madam stood white and nervous and ill at ease near the door, and Lady Callerley kept her seat by old Nanny, and spoke no word; while she was considering the question of what was the right course to adopt under the circumstances. Did ye come to see us, or did ye expect to find company here, Mrs. Breamish ?" asked the fisher- girl, deliberately. Madam pointed to the door. "I saw the horse—your Britomart, Lady Cal- lerley," she said, with considerable hesitation, "I obeyed a sudden impulse—l scarce knew why ! save that I have heard or seen nothing of any one from Seaton Callerley for so long, and—' here she paused, and looked furtively at Silvia. It appeared to the latter to see very singular the clever woman of the world so ill at ease. Even Bell, who mistrusted her as much as ever, wondered what the meaning of it could be. Lady Callerley rose from her seat and advanced towards Madam, as though to shake hands. But Bell interposed. " Dinna hey owt te say te her, Laddy Callerley," she entreated, with unconquerable suspicion, " she's worked ye more mischief nor ye're aware of!

"I can forgive it all, since it has failed in its object! Oh, Bell, why should I be hard upon her, now that I have all I wish for in the world !" asked Lady Callerley in a sweet, pleading voice. "Ye dinna know, or ye wadn't be so keen of forgiving." Madam seized Bell's arm, and gazed beseech- ingly into her stern face. "I mean no harm to her or to anyone," she whispered, "have mercy, and hold your tongue; if not for my sake, then most certainly for hers. You shall hear all I have to say, and I ask no more than to be allowed to say it." Bell wavered a little. As she stood there doubt- ful, old Nanny, who had been a silent observer of the scene, suddenly spoke out of her corner. "Let her alone, Bell, ma woman! She's one o' the family, an' hes a right to be heard, whatever her faults may be ! An' if they're apart i' joy, they'll mebbe be linked tigither sorrow yet. Speak on, Madam Breamish, but beware o' sayin' owt but the truth, or ye'll dearly rue the day !' Madam must indeed have been changed, since even this speech of the old woman failed to arouse any haughty indignation in her. "It is not much I have to ask Lady Callerley, and I think she is too kind-hearted to refuse me such &small favour. My boy—little Lance, whom you have in past times professed some fondness for —he is ill, and wearying for a sight of you! Ever since his uncle Jack, to whom, as you may remern- ber, he is fondly attached, left the place, he has fretted and pined, and refused to be comforted. The doctor tells me he will never get strong, but will sink into a decline unless we can rouse him to take interest in something, and—and when I , mentioned your name, the boy's face brightened at once, and he begged to be taken to you: calling you his pretty angel, aed saying that pin would be sure to love him again now when he was ill !" "Poor little Lance 1" ejaculated Silvia, pitifully. "Therefore I sought this oottage," went on Mrs. Breamish in a hard meshaaWd• sort of way, as though it were a lesson she was repeating, "mean- ing to send a message or a letter by Bell IViddring- ton, but since I have been fortunate enough to find you here. I make my appeal to you by words inetead "'What is it you wish me to do ?" asked Lady Callerley at once. "I am very sorry, very sorry indeed, for the poor little boy, but my husband has refused to allow math visit Breamish, and I must not vex him by disobedience. And yet he would surely not be angry if he knew the facts Of elle case ?—the dear little loving heart--No, no, I must e'en brave his anger to save the child." As she mused aloud in kindness and perplexity of spirit, Bell gave a significant look at Madam. "DO you hear her ?" she asked in a low tone, "she would even vex her man, him that she loves 8o well, to please ye, and to save your bBirn ! Ye best ken whether ye deserve such fair dealins at her hands ?" "No, no, you must not go against Lancelot in anything," cried Madam hastily, "I did not mean that at all ! But do not you think that if he knew —he was ever kind to the lad, and took a good deal of noti;:e of him in every way, the lad who favours him in features too—oh, do you not think he would allow you to come, or even allow us to send him to you for a few hours now and then ; just until he grows more interested in things, and ceases to fret after Jack? Think, Lady Callerley, he is my only child !" or the first time the liar voice softened slightly, and a note of anguish pierced through the even monotony of it. "And has not Lady Callerley lost her only , child ?" asked the fisher girl, still with consider- able sternness.

"Ah yes ; but she is young, while I—if he dies there is nothing left to me ! It is not because he loves me, for even in his illness he turns away peevishly when I come near. I have not the gift of winning love. All those who have been nearest to my heart turn from me and scorn the affection I proffer. So be it 1 Anti yet it would be hard to see him die." "He shall not die if we can save him. Bell, you must let me speak! I am promising nothing that is wrong. My husband is too good to deny me such a simple matter. I shall send for Lance to-morrow, or perhaps—who knows—Lancelot may ride over himself and bring him back." "No, not that !" cried Madam, cowering and trembling at the very thought of again meeting the man who had treated her with just contempt and righteous indignation. "I cannot—l dare not meet Lancelot."

_ "Why ?" asked Lady Callerley, surprised at the emotion displayed by her husband's cousin.' I "Anything but that I am afraid of him. Don't look so astonished, Silvia! We—we quarel- led when last we met—that is all! But to see those eyes which I have—loved to look upon from —childhood, full of scorn and loathing—l could not bear it, and--.-it sends me mad—l feel them burn into my brain." "Poor woman! There is no doubt of her being more than a little insane," thought Lady Callerley with pity; while Bell Widdrington,with consider- able shrewdness, guessed the truth. "There is no need of either Sir Lancelot or Leddy Callerley gannin' te Bramish," decided the fisher girl at one!. gie fetch him. hie th

morn's- day, an' then he can be sent for fra' Seaton Callerley." Eventually this mode of action was decided upon ; and just in time, for the sound of the trotting of Sir Lancelot's horse was heard in the distance.

Mrs, Breamish evinced great perturbation at the idea that he might enter and had her there ; but Lady Callerley reassured her by preferring to meet him outside, when he would not be likely to care about entering. "You may rely on me," she said on parting, "I will send for the lad to-morrow, since the doctor thinks the change might be beneficial." Madam listened in silence to the joyous greet- ing between husband and wife, and saw them ride off togther right gaily. . If the miserable woman felt an added pang at this pleasant spectacle, she certainly showed no sign of it. "She is a deal better to ye than aw should ha' been in her place," commented Bell with severity. "If ye dinna feel ashamed an' guilty efter such kindness, then ye're getten' ne feelins left, aw reckon."
" Feelings ? What have I ,to do with feelings now, foolish girl? Is it not all a dead world to me from henceforth.

"A deid world, say ye?" ejaculated old Nanny Widdrington in a shrill treble tone, which made itself heard above all the noise of the rushing of water coining through the open door. "Ay, it will be a deid world in very truth to ye, an' te me, an' te her that's just gaen oot o' yon door! Divvent ye hear it comin', Dorothy Breamish, fleein' aleng the wind, an' tearin' doon wi' the water o' YArrop? It'll not be long or the air'll resound wi' the cries o' the widow an' the childless. Listen, aw tell ye, Madam, for ye're one o' the fated brood, an' the curse is on you an yours. Wee' may ye say it's a deid world. It's the truest word ye've ever said in all yer life, though you little think it !" As she finished aFeaking, the strange emotional mood which had strengthened and inspired her passed from the sibyl: and she fell back into her arm chair exhausted.

In a moment she seemed to, shrivel up. and be- come again the feeble half-witted old creature of the past few months. Feebly she held out her shaking hand; and Bell divining her want, gave her a little Hollands gin in a tumbler with some hot water, and after a while she fell into a doze, worn out with her prophetic utterances. Madam was greatly impressed with these same utterances.
Had she not herself wished for a storm to come, a storm of disaster and misery? What if her wicked invocation had been sue. cesaful
CHAPTER LANCE AND HIS MOTHER.

"Lancelot," said Lady Callerley timidly, when the married pair had ridden some way homeward, I have something to tell you, dear? Who do you think was at the cottage yonder, when I came out to you l" Sir Lancelot darted a quick glance at her. "How should I know, ? Not—surely, that woman • after all that passed between us can- not have dared to approach you?" And his dark brows met in a most portentous frown. "Do not be angry, Lancelot. She did not know that I was within until she saw Britomart standing by the door; and then she could not resist coming to ask me herself! And do you know I was actually sorry for her, and liked her better than ever before ; and she is so changed, so worn and old-looking, and then after all, you know, she is his mother—"

" What are you talking about, Silvia? You must really try and be more consecutive, if you mean rue to understand you 1" Lady Callerley was nervous and excited, and her words certainly came with a confusing rush. But the marked coldness of her husband's manner checked her impetuosity at once.

"Pardon me, dear! You know lam only a silly little creature, but I will try to explain matters. You must not be vexed because I listened to what she had to say !" The pretty, pleading tone was irresistible; but Sir Lancelot, while he smiled in answer to it, was evidently very seriously annoyed at the recontre. She ought to have respected my wishes, and to have kept away from you! My blood boils at the idea that she should dare to be with you, to touch your hand, to breathe the same atmosphere even! A woman like that—good heavens! She is not fit to approach—" "Don't, Lancelot, you know you promised not to be angry !" remonstrated Lady Callerley. "What did ahe say? Did she try to make fur- ther mischief ?"

"This is beyond her power, dear husband !" said Silvia tenderly, her eyes meeting those of Sir Lancelot in perfect love and trust. "No, it was nothing of that sort! Nor—since you seem to care about it—did I even go so far as to shake hands with her. Bell interposed and would not allow me so to do. Indeed, Bell was quite as determined about.that as you appear to be. You are too bitter, I think! What makes you so hard and unforgiv- ing, Lancelot ?" The Baronet flushe'd and looked discomposed. "You must trust my deciaion when I tell you it is for the beet that you two should not meet ; " he replied, rather vaguely; and you have not yet told me what she had to say?" "It was a favour she begged of me—end of you! The boy—dear little Lance—whom you have always appeared fond of, is i// ; has fretted himself ill since his uncle Jack went away ; and now she says he wishes to see me, and the doctor thinks it would do him good to come toSeaton Callerley and —and oh, Lancelot, I felt so sorry about it, that I promised he should pay us a visit, and now I am afraid you will be cross !" Sir Lancelot rode on in silence for some time, and Silvia's lips quivered. She had grown used to happiness, and the least discord hurt her. "I could not help it," she said, with tears in her eyes; "I can't bear to think of the lonely, tender, little heart longing for love—" "Has lie not an affectionate mother to pet and coddle him," asked Sir Lancelot in a bitter sort of Way...

Ah, thqre's where it is! That is what makes my heart ache for her, false though she may have been to me! The boy turns from her, and refuses to he comforted for the loss of poor Jack. She has not the power of winning love, she declares I" Then Silvia leant across and touched her hus- band's arm. _ _

" Lancelot I have been a mother, and I know what keenest ago-ny that would be And it ia surely a sign of better things that she can init aside any natural feeling of jealousy she may have, and beg my kindness for her boy? Think of it, dear. Such a proud woman as she is!"

"Silvia, you are too good for this world! I believe that even if you knew the depth of infamy to which that woman has sunk, you would, never- theless, still find a word to say in extenuation of hi+ sins! Have it your own way, dear child! You have conquered. I will myself ride over for the lad to-morrow. Will that content you r Lady Callerley explained the arrangement which had been made, and that it would be unnecessary for him to go further than the Widdrington's cottage, where the boy would be brought to meet him.
"She is afraid of you—Dorothy Breamish is afraid of you ! You must have been very severe with her when you two met last. How was it you never told me of your visit to Breamish Lancelot?"

" There was not much totell, save that she showed herself in her true colours, and that I hated her for it ! But it is well that she should yet have some shame left !" Then Sir Lancelot changed the subject hastily, and declined further questioning upon it.

*• - - Little Lance was wild with excitement and delight when he heard the news that he was to go to Seaton Callerley. In bed that night he loqked up at the picture of the 'angel which to his fancy resembled his dear, beautiful Lady Callerley, and once again it seemed to wear its old, sweet, loving smile. "I am coming to you to-morrow," he said, in his childish treble, "and you must love me again like you used to do, and we will play games to- gether—not only in the picture gallery, because they say the old lord comes there sometimes, and stops again to look at the picture he was looking at when he fell down in a fit and died. I knew all about it; but Uncle Jack was cross with me for mentioning it to Cousin Silvia; though, after all, I did not tell her why I wouldn't play there I Oh, dear, I wish Uncle Jack was to be there too. Never mind, I can talk about him to my pretty lady.' Mother Os not fond of him, so I am obliged to hold my tongue ; though it's dread- fully hard to do it when I miss him so." Some unwonted impulse had drawti the mother he spoke of to his room just at that time and through the half-opened door she had hasid his aoliimuY•

"She put her hand to her side, as though a sud- den pang smote her. "Jack and Silvia, the two I have so hated, have completely stolen his heart between them, and taken my place in his affection. And yet I cannot deny the justice of it. The good and the innocent draw together, the wicked and the guilty alone are solitary for ever !" With her soft, noiseles4 step she went up to- the bedside, and stood there looking down at her boy.

Little Lance at that moment, his cheeks flushed and his eyes bright as stars, looking up in astoni§h- inent at her sudden entrance, appeared beautiful exceedingly. His indisposition had fined down his features and the exuberant vitality which was their marked characteristic, and the consequence was that just then his face was infinitely more angelic than the pictured one above him. "Have you no love left for me—your mother— Lance ?" asked Mrs. Breamish, with more gentle- ness than was usual to her.

The boy looked at her wistfully. There was a sadness in her voice that touched his childish sympathies, far more keenly than the ordinary fierce and jealous reproach which generally under- lay such utterances:

Yes, mother—since you care, I will love you dearly," he answered in a timid, hesitating way. Mrs. Breamish sat down upon the bed and clasped the boy to her heart, in a much softer and more caressing manner than usual. With quick response, Lance put his soft little arms around her neck, and they clung together there, mother and child, in a tender, loving embrace. These few blissful and innocent moments, when she could feel the beating of that child's heart upon her own, and the touch of the clinging arms about her neck; coming across her clouded memory after- wards were as a glimpse of a lost paradise to a soul suffering the torments of the damned. "You are different to-night, mammy dear," said the boy at length, patting her cheek in pretty babyish fashion, "sometimes I am afraid of you, and that is why I dare not love you too much. Why are you not always like this; soft and sweet, and letting me cuddle into you in the same way Juno's puppies do to her? Do you know I have often wished I were a puppy, when I looked at them there all happy together !" Madam answered nothing, but held him closer to her breast. There was a tightness and an aching pain there, which the pressure seemed to relieve. • "Do you not want me to go to Seaton Callerley, mother ?" Lance went on, after a moment's pause, "I do not care so much about it, now that you are nice !"
Dorothy Breamish's arms relaxed, and she stood upright._
'FO'r a few minutes she had forgotten everything, save that she was a mother.
But at the mention of Seaton Callerley, it came back; and she was no longer a simple woman, with a child's heart beating against her own. She sighed, and passed her hand across her brow.

"Good-night, dear Lance ! You may sleep now, or you will be too tired to get up to-morrow. Remember, your pretty Lady Callerley with be grievously disappointed if you cannot bear the journey! "Kiss me good-night, then !" pleaded the boy; and for the last time the lips of mother and child met. For the last time, though neither of them knew it then.

In the morning there was hurry and confusion. The Squire was going a-hunting, and required a considerable amount of attention from everyone. During the excitement little Lance left without his farewell kiss.
(To be eoritinued).

div.head: TRAGIC LOVE STORY.
div.p: TRAGIC LOVE STORY.

A tragic tale of disapppointed love is told us by Vienna correspondent. At Phillippopolis,in Eastern Roumelia, a Bulgarian officer, Major Liopopetoff, and the daughter of a rich Greek merchant. M. Kalamides, had fallen in love, but the father ob- jected to their marriage, because as a Greek, he would not hear of a 13u1gar1an son-in-law. The other day he formally forbade the match. A few hours later he took a walk with his wife and daughter. ill the public promenade, when they met the The latter diew his revolver; and to shoot down father, mother,and daughter was the work of a few second ra s. Then he drew his sword and stabbed hi- sell through the heart. He ex 0ir,41 on the spot, and the father has already succumbed to his wound. The mother and daughter are still alive, but their condition is hopeless. raajor.

div.head: STRANGE FREAK.
div.p: A STRANGE FREAK.

There is living on a farm within five =riles of Forsythe, in America, one of the strangest freaks that have ever been heard of. The freak is the son or daughter, or both, of James Howard, a farmer. There is • perfect double child of both sexes, but connected in such a way that no possible surgical operation can separate them. The children are now seven years old. They are perfectly formed with the exception that they have about eight inches of spinal column in common. They are back to back, and about ten inches above the end of the spinal columns the bones merge into one columm with a single spinal cord. The bodiea separate again, and the lower parts are entirely dis- tinct. Howard has been approached several times by museum men who have heard of the freak, but he steadily refuses all offers to exhibit the children.. The children play and act as other children, of their age do,. and seem in no wise affected by their singu- lar situation. They have much difficulty in loco- motion, but they have hit on a plan of their own whereby they get about. They have an understancling,and when one wants to go forward the other is told, ant walks back- ward. They have done this so much that they can walk either way very readily. They have no thoughts in common,and are apparently thoroughly distinct, with the exception of the slight confla- tion of their spines.

It was not an idea that seemed very likely of realisation, for the difficulties are many'. Nl"' hix—Aunt Martha as they call her—is old,and 'the little negro republic on the West Coast of Africa is a long saY off. " But my time was nearly over," she .says for 1. am seventy-six, and though they told me that never come I must see the Queen now or never shall I see her. And so I should have come if it had been but by myself alone." She did indeed set out from Liberia by herself, with no guide and no credential of her Iris' Sion, except a satin quilt, embroidered with a pattern of the coffee plant, which she hoped the Queen might take from her. But although Mrs. Ria did indeed set out on her pil- grimage alone, she did not make the journey by herself. for she was accompanied by Mrs. Roberts, the wife of an I ex-President of Liberia, and on her arrival in England I Dr. Blyden, the Liberian Minister, interested himself in the furtherance of her desire. He wrote last week ta Sir Henry Ponsonby, telling him of the arrival in Eng- land of Mrs. Blyden. and asking that she should be allowed to present Mrs. Martha Rix, whose little story he detailed. Sir Henry Ponsonby replied, suggesting an unofficial visit, eince the necessity for applying for as official visit through the Foreign Office would take time, and on Saturday a telegram asked Mrs. Blyden to bring Mrs. Rix with her. On the arrival of the party from Liberia at Windsor, they were taken to the Castle in three of the Queen's carriages. Mrs. Blyden, her augh ter, her littlegranddaughter, and Mrs. Rix were received at the door of her Palace by the Master of the Household who escorted them to the Royal. presence. The ClUeen received her guests surrounded by her own children and grandchildren, the Prince and Princess of Wales, Prine,ess Louise, Princess Beatrice, and the Princesses Victoria and Maud. Each of the guests was presented to the Queen, who shook hands with them, an said some gra- cious words to each. To the old lady who had come so- I far to see her, the Queen said that she felt " greatly. honoured by the trouble you have taken to come ta. visit me ;" and to the youngest of the Liberians spoke with an affectionate and characteristic kindlisegs. For Mrs. Rix—this has been the great, the only dalr her life. "I cannot tell what she said to me,' she ssY.9.. speaking of her visit; "but the Queen spoke very an". and I think she must have been saying blessings 50 I shall now, after a time, go back to my country. no that I have done seeing the Queen, and I shall alwaY/ remember. I came to Ene.land thinking, perhaps. might see her; plenty of friends have I found here, an" have seen her who is our Mother. That I shall reMesl7 her in the dAys which go by before the time shall be tot sleep,"

The monthly session of the No. 1 Convention South Lance,shire. Good •Templars was held at Etatles-' town, on Saturday, in the Wesleyan Leetatre Bro. Colour-Sergeant Mantle, C.C.T., of Warringtsn, preside& The Tress and credential committee hoc.- ing been appointed, the mutates of the Last sessiamt, held at Widnes. were read and corefirmed. The roll of off, cers was called, and the reportc were submitted. Ern. Roberts C.C., tin.regard to the Warrington lodges, re- ported that the attendances were not quite as satisfac- tory as could be W:ohed, and this it was thought was ' due to the summer .season and outside attractions, this being also borne out by Bro. It. Zean, C. Sec. No re- port was submitted in regard to the Young 40th Lodge, but the other lodges., such as Ashton, Earlestown, Firs- lane, and Wesley we in a satisfactory condition. Other business was transacted, and fit was stated that a distinct promise had been obtaine&from Mr.Seton-Karr, M.P., to support direct veto and Cunday closing, at which satisfaction was apressed. The various reports were adopted. It was stated that TiVidnes and Peasley Cross lodges required help from the (Convention, and it was decided to hold meetings, a ,committee being appointed to arrange. The next place of meeting was f..ated for" Excelsior' Lodge, Ashtou, oa August 20th. Bro. J. Brockbank, C. Trea. introduced for discussion, the question of opening up new fields and the improve- ment of old ground. The discussion was taken part in by Bros. Clarke, Mantle, and Roberts, and it was decided to leave the extension of Good Ternplary into new fields, over until the Sept eis ber Session.—Tbe session afterwards closed in the usual manner.—The delegates., repsesenta- Oyes* and others then partook of a well served tea, after which a public meeting was held in the Wesleyan School- room. Bro. Mantle D.C.T., presided and there was a good attendance.—Bro. J. Vint, L.D.. of Ashton, delivered an interesting address upon the temperance question, and alluded to the fact that the representatives of tem- perance in the House of Commons had considerably in- creased. which would strengthen the hands of their leader, Sir W. Lawson. Their good cause which was mainly directed to the elevation of mankind was pro- gressing, and many bad been lifted from a low position to one of prominence, and credit to themselves and their neighbours.—Bro. M. Jones D.C.T., of Liverpool, also addressed the gathering and said that as good Templars they were in the midst of a great struggle. They must be consistent, and not parley with evil. It must be war to the knife and the knife must be buried to the hilt. The result of the drink traffic was to drag men down from the highest positions of Society. They must go out to those who needed their help, and always hoped to get what they asked for, and to do this they must go into their work with spirit and determination.—Bro. W. Blair also gave an encoura g,ing, address, and at intervals songs , glees, recitations, and readings were given by members. At the close the usual votes of thanks were accorded the chairman and visitors. AMUSEMENT ON THE RAILWAY.

THE POLLING

took place on Monday. The number of electors on the register is 11,750, but the effective voting strength would be under 11,000. The polling com- menced at eight a.m, in twelve polling districts, and Mr. W. Handley was assisted in his duties of Liberal agent by the following sub-agents:—ish- ton-by-Sutton, Mr. Thomas Leach; Barnton and Weaverham, Mr. W. C. Deakin; Nrorthwich Castle and Witton, Mr. J. J. Dickson; Marston, Mr. George i E., King; Middlewich, Mr. James Williams; Run- corn North and South, Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys; and Winsford, Mr. W. H. Tolfree. For the Conser- vatives Mr. C. Hughes, the agent, had appointed the following sub-agents: Barnton, Mr. James Grimshaw; Davenham, Mr. Richard L Fryer; Marston, Mr. R. G. Stanley Banks.; Middlewich, Mr. F. B. Cooke; Northwich Castle, Mr. William Bancroft; Northwich Witton, Mr. G. A. Hughes; Runcorn North, Mr. J. W. Lightburn ; Runcorn South and Ashton, Mr. A. Lightburn ; Weaverham, Mr. William Henry Rushes; Winsford, Mr. Joseph Parkinson. Each candidate had a host of workers throughout the division, and there was a great dis- play of party favours. A great amount of interest was centred in the proceed- ings at Northwich. All the morning matters were quiet and orderly. The voting was, however, exceedingly active, especially between eight and nine, owing chiefly to the fact that a large number of eight hours' shift men commence the day at Messrs. Brunner., Mond, and Co.'s works at ten a.m. After 9-30 there was a lull, but between twelve and one business was again brisk. From six p.m. to the closing hour there was an increased flow of voters into the polling booths. As the afternoon ad- vanced, a good deal of excitement prevailed lathe streets, particularly in the vicinity of the committee rooms of the candidates; but there was no disorder of any conse- quence. Colonel Hamersley, the chief constable, with Superintendent Hindley, of Birkenhead, was in the town, and had command of sufficient force of police. officers to quell any disturbance that might arise. After the close of the poll, the ballot boxes were deposited by the presiding officers at the police station. The Liberals entertained a very strong feeling that Mr. Brunner had been returned by a very decisive majority. At eight 1 o'clock Mr. and Mrs. Brunner drove into Northwich in an open barouche, amidsttremendous cheering. Entering the Gladstone Club
MR.. BRIZINNI'My

after prolonged scenes of indescribable anthusiasm,said : Well, gentlemen, you have done splendid work to-day. (Loud cheers, and a voice " IWO majority.") Mr. Brunner continuing: I am an old hand at this game. (Hear, hear.) I have been at it since 1865, and that is 27 years, and I never in my life saw as good a record as Ithere is here to-day. (Loud cheers.) I have a telegram 1 here from Middiewich which says that they have polled 721, of whom 519 are Liberals and 262 are Conservatives. (Loud cheers.) I have had nothing to eat since break- fast, and now I should like something cool. (Laugtter.) The best wish I can wish you all is that I hope you will sleep as well as I shall to-night. (Loud cheers.)

div.p: HR. WHITELEY.

.As-soon as the poll had been closed, Mr. and Mrs. WlrKstiey, with Mr. Joseph Verdin and Mr. T. Ward, visited the Constitutional Club, where they were most warmly welcomed by the crowd of people there assembled. Amid ringing cheers, the Conservative can-. didate•said he hoped if they happened to have been beater they would not been disappointed. He heartily thanked -the workers for what they had done, and the enthusiastic manner in which they had carried on the election. Fr. less than twelve months he believed there would be.cnother election, and ha was quite ready to fight again. (Cheers.) After thanking and conversing with severAl workers, Mr. and Mrs. Whiteley left the club and entyred their cArriage. On the way to Hart- ford they were cheered and hooted. AL Ha ncore the greatest Interest was manifested. The !arose town id the division, it has a voting strength of

one-third of the wleati division. In Runcorn North there are 2,447 names on the register and lie Runcorn South 1,169. For the convenience of voters there were seven polling stations. Of these five were at the Market Hall in Bridge-st., and two were at the Board School ha Victoria-road. Beyond vehicles being rapidly driven to and fro, there was nothing to indicate that anything I unusual was taking place, but in the neighbourhood of the polling booths, where the respective parties had also their committee rooms, all was bustle and animation. The voting was very steady up to noon,about 300 having voted at Runcorn South and 600 at Runcorn north. Mr. Whiteley, accompanied by his wife, arrived early in the town, and visited the Committee rooms,where he busied himself in seeing that the organisation WAS in good order and in taking voters to the poll. In the course ot the morning Mr. and Mrs. Whiteley were driven throue.h the town in an open carriage, and the partisans showed their feelings by cheering and hooting. About eleven o'clock Mr. and Mrs. Whiteley departed for Northwich. In the afternoon Mr. and Mrs. Brunner arrived by train and were driven in an open carriage through the streets. Mr. P. Speaktnan, C.C., accompanied the candidate and his wife. At Runcorn North Committee room, Mr. Brunner delivered a speech to the assembled hundreds.

MR. BRUNNER AT RUNCORN. Mr. Brunner said : Ladies and gentleman,—As I have just come from the country, I suppose you have all heard the news before me. We have won a magnificent victory in West Denbighshire. Here is a gentleman who was a Liberal in 1885, at the very high tide of Liberaliqn got a majority of 1,700, and in 1888, when be was a Unionist, he was returned unopposed. Now he has been upset by a majority far larger than the one he obtained in 1885. The magnificent figure obtained by Mr. Herbert Roberts (Gladstonian) over Mr. Cornwallis West (Unionist) is 2,333. Now, gentlemen, I ask that you keep the road to the polling stations open, so that it shall not be blockaded by strangers. 'rake care there is a road open to the polling booth, and see to it that no one interferes, and then make sure that everyone of your friends who can get there before seven o'clock shall do so, as it is between that hour and the close of the poll that the mischief will be done, and I trust to you, as earnest and true Liberals, to prevent it. (Cheers, and a voice, " lain a Liberal.") I have very little doubt, ladies and gentlemen, that if you all spoke the sentiments of your hearts, you would cry with this lady "I am a Liberal." (Laughter.) Take care from five o'clock until eight o'clock you are ready to bring men to the poll and help them to get in. I ask this as a final effort for the good old cause of Liberalism, and when that is done my majority will not be far short of that at West Denbigh- shire. (Cheers.) I have addressed many great gather- ings of my fellow voters in Runcorn, and I hope, ladies and gentlemen, that you will give me many another opportunity of addressing you as your representative. I am one of the old-fashioned sort, who will not, as soon as the election is over, go and leave you. (Cheers.) I am bound to be amongst you during the rest of my days, and I hope I shall continue in the character of a neigh- bour, as your representative. (Cheers.) We will wish to Mr. Whiteley a happy return to Blackburn. (Cheers.) Mr. Brunner afterwards was driven through the various polling places into Northwich. After tea the polling became very brisk, and there were large crowds in the vicinity of the two polling places, but the utmost good humour prevailed, and there was not throughout the day a case of disturbance. Superintendent Ather- ton had taken the precaution to draft in an extra force of constables, but the ordinary staff proved quite cap- able of dealing with the traffic. After the polls closed at eight o'clock, it was believed that the heaviest poll yet taken in the division had been recorded,and the chances of the two candidates wete eagerly discussed. It was generally believed amongst the Liberals that Mr. Brunner had won by a handsome majority.

GREAT LIBERAL VICTORY.. The counting of the votes took place at the Central 1 Central Hall, Northwich, on Tuesday, a consummation ,1 which was intensely grateful to all concerned after a lona 11 drawn contest fought with a keeness probably not ex- ceeded throughout the kingdom. The presiding officer was Mr. Cullitnore, of Chester, the acting Under-Sheriff. The Chief Constable of the county was also present with a considerable body of police, A very heavy rainstorm, which continued from early morning all through the torenoon,rendered the lot of those gathered to await the declaration of the poll extremely uncomfortable, as no shelter whatever was availanle. Nevertheless, the avenue leading to the Central Hall was crowded, and the people very patiently took the soaking which re- sulted from their exposure to the driving rain. It was about twenty minutes past twelve when the doors were opened, and the Acting-Under-Sheriff (Mr. J. Cullimore) announced the result, which was—

div.head: J. T. BRUNNER L.... 5580
div.p: J. T. BRUNNER L.... 5580
G. WHrTELEY C 4325

Liberal Majority.... 1:25-1 The crowd hearing the name of Mr. Brunner first, at once gave vent to tremendous cheering, which was carried along up the streets towards the Gladstone Club, as if by electricity. Inside the hall the candidates, both of whom had witnessed the counting, which com- menced at 9-30, now stayed to perform the usual courtesies. MR. BRUNNER ON HIS VICTORY.

Mr. Brunner then entered his carriage, and drove to the Gladstonian Club amidst a scene of tremendous enthusiasm, the streets,notwithstanding the still heavily • falling rain being crowded with people ' cheering the member. The carriage with difficulty made its way through the crowd, and Mr. Brunner, alighting, was pushed through the mass of people into the club, which was thronged with Liberal workers. After a prolonged storm of cheers both inside and outside the Mr. Brunner, appearing on the balcony of the club with Mrs. Brunner, said—My neighbours—(cheers)—ln 1885 you defeated the candidate who came here as the representative of a trade in your district. Mr. William Henry Verdin stood as the representative of the salt trade. I stood as the representative of all. (Cheers.) Mr. Verdin was the representative of the local trade. In 1892 you have defeated the representative of another , trade and not a local trade. (Cheers.) You have defeated at this election the power of the brewers,which has done enormous mischief at this election. (" Hear, hear "and cheers.) And I congratulate you that you have defeated the power of the brewers' representative. (Cheers.) You have elected me in spite et the opposi- tion.—(A Voice "We will do it again")---of the territo- rial interest, and against the representative of the Duke of Westminster. (Groans.) (A voice : " What are the figures ?") I will give them to you. Five years ago your vote for me was 5112 ;it is this time 5580. (Loud cheers.) Lord Henry Grosvenor polled 3933 and Mr. Whiteley has polled 4325. (Groans.) The ma- jority last time was 1129, and this time it is 1255. (Cheers.) Last month the leader of the House of Commons came here to oppose me, and you have sent to Mr.Balfour,the representative of a defeated Government, a fit and proper answer. (Cheers.) In Northwich, at any rate, you have proved that a prophet bath honour in his own country. (Cheers.) We have conducted this contest throughout in thorough good humour as befits those who are going to win. (Cheers.) After fighting we are going to retain our good humour and be friends with our enemies here. (Cheers.) As I said to an enormous crowd at Runcorn yesterday, " A happy return to Blackburn to Mr. Whiteley." (Pro- longed cheering.) Immediately the result was declared. Mr. Whiteley, amid cheers and counter cheers, proceeded to the Con- stitutional Club, where a good number of his supporters had gathered. Mr. Thomas Ward, J.P., who had fre- quently addressed meetings during the contest on behalf of Mr. Whiteley's candidature, stated that they were not to be disheartened by the result, as Mr. Brunner had only increased his majority by about 103 out of an increased poll of a thousand. They had also to take linto consideration that during the past few days the election all over the country had been against them, and that probably had had an effect upon the contest.

IN THE GLADSTONE CLUB. Mr. Brunner afterwards addressed those gathered in the clubroom, and said that election had been a victory for the people over privilege. (Applause.) They as Liberals desired for one thing that the privilege of gov- erning the liquor trade should be taken Out QI the hands of a few magistrates and given into the hands of those who rightly ought to have the control, the people themselves. (Applause.) The victory of that day was one of the finest over the liquor trade that had occurred in the country. (Applause.) He must thank them all most heartily, and he would say that whether he was living at London or at Druid's cross, Northwich would be very near his heart. (Loud applause.) Mr. A. Mond said they had fought a good fight, and had won a sound victory. They must keep up their organisation, so that neither the most desperate nor most dispicable attempts to wrest the seat from them would succeed. (Applause.) Mr. .1. F. L. Brunner complimented them upm their splendid organisation, and said theae was not a man in the town unaccounted for. They wou!d go on in7reas- ing the majority every time that seat was contested. (Applause.) Mr. Samuel Harrison said he rejoiced, both ac a work- ing-man and a trades unionist, at Mr. Brunner's return. (Applause.) Mr. Brunner was afterwards drawn in his carriage, together with Mrs. Brunner and li!s two thughters, to Winnington Hall, his admirers being willing steeds. MR. BRUNNER AT RUNCORN.—TRIUMPHAL PROGRESS.

It was expected that the result would become known about half-past twelve, hut long blfore that time the Liberal Club was crowded with Mr. Hrunner's enthusia, - tic supporters waiting for the tidings. That ti ey were of great inr, they did no: doubt for oi e ,tnoobriei e tidingsn d they spent the time in lustily sinAng the election songs composed by Mr. Handley. About quarter to one o'clock the telegram was receivt d, t e numb:lrs being read out, and a ao-rta of unboundexi en- thusiasm ensued, and a shout of triumph went up that I must have reached the committee room of tho oppsitior. :-liortiv after five o'cleck th succ. ssful eand doe dr into the town, he was met v. the outskirts by a great crowd. The pair of hor.es were quick y unyoked, ropes attached to the carriage,and a number of stalwart fellows pulled it through the town. Mr. P. Speakman was with
Mr. Brunner. A halt was made at the Liberal Club, where .i. large crowd. had assembled, and . . _

Mr. Speakman publicly congratulated Mr. Brunner on his triumphant reiurn. He said: Ladies and gentle- men, I am in the proud position to-day of introducing to you our member of Parliament, Mr. Brunner. (Cheers.) I thank you on behalf of the Liberal party for the very magnificent way in which you have done your duty. Mr. Brunner has represented you in Parlia- ment in the past, and it is a proud position for him awl for you that he is going to represent you in the future. (Cheers.) Addressing the great assemblage of people, Mr. Brun- ner said : lam once more your representative. (Cheers.) I am not the member for the brewers, but for the people. (Cheers.) We have beaten Mr. Balfour' the Duke of Westminster, the trades' unions of Irish land- lords, the great brewing interest, and the Blackburn personators. (Cheers.) I thank you for the glorious work you have done at this election. lam at all times ready to cheer for Runcorn, which is the backbone of Liberalism in the constituency. Runcorn polled well in 1887, but she has done splendidly in 1892. The election has been won in spite of the foulest aspersions cast upon my personal character. (Cheers.) I have been accused of coercing the men employed at Winnington, but there is no truth in it. I wish that the working-men altt over the country were as free in their po- litical opinions and speech as those connected with the firm of Brunner Mond and Co. (Cheers.) I wish prosperity to Runcorn, and I hope the time will come, and that soon, when the great United Alkali Company may follow Brunner, Mond, and Co., in giving an eight hours day to those engaged by them. (Cheers.) lam going back to London in a few days, and there I shall meet new friends, for we have turned out no less than 55 Tories to replace them with Liberals. (Cheers.) Once again, and for the fourth time Mr. Gladstone was going to be Prime Minister of England. He is the noblest leader that ever party had, the noblest servant that ever sovereign had, the noblest chieftain that ever nation had, and I am proud to appear before this multi- tude as a devoted follower of the Grand Old Man. (Cheers.) Afterwards Mr. Brunner addressed the workers in the club. He thanked them heartily for their efforts, and said he had received many congratulations from all over the country. He assured them that the victory of 1892 had given no less pleasure than the one of 1887. (Cheers.) He hoped to live to deserve their support. The Tories had done their level best to beat him, but the result showed that he was firmer in the affection of his friends than ever. Had he been ready to make a cor- rupt bargain to prevent opposition he could have done so' for if he would have promised that there should not bea fight in the Knutsford Division he had the assurance that there should not be one in Northwich. (Cheers.)
Other speeches were made, and then Mx Brunner was again drawn through the town, amid one continual round of cheering.

div.head: SONGS FOR THE PEOPLE.
div.p: SONGS FOR THE PEOPLE.

NO. I.—THE LIQUOR TRAFFIC. Working-men where'er ye be, Toiling on the land and sea, Join us in a grand crusade: For the countless wrongs of years, For its victims' groans and tears, War we with the Liquor Trade. In " Bar Parlours" snug and warm, Where the favoured topers swarm, And their souls with drink delight : There vain babblings loud and long, With stale jests and roaring song, Rudely mock the peaceful night. Workhouses with paupers crammed, Wretches in our prisons damned,
Drink's infernal produce show: And in madhouse cells confined Crowds of beings wreck'd in mind,

Swell" the bottle's "crop of woe. Down in slums and alleys foul, Drunkards in their misery howl, And with curses fill the air: While, of every comfort shorn, Starving wives and children mourn In the blackness of despair. 0 my fellow-workers, rise. Let these horrid sights and cries Urge ye to be swift and brave : NOW's your day and now's your hour, .„ In your will there lies the power From Drinka curse our land to save.. From the Council Chambers clear All the nominees of beer, And the grog-men drive away, That the Liquor Laws in force May have free, unfetter'd course, To effect what good they may. Then when Whigs and Tories blue Would your vote and interest woo,. For some fav'rite partisan ; Vote for him, and him alone, Who will make your cause his own.

And strong drink for ever band' Down with Bacchus with a run, Foulest god beneath the sun. All his seething temples raze ; And in mills or on the soil, Tarn his priests to honest toil, For the remnant of their days.
MYRA.
DEATH OF LORD LATHOM'S MOTHER.

The death took place last evening, at Blythe Hall,. Ormskirk, in her 90th year, of Jessie, widow of the Hon. Richard Bootle Wilbraham, and mother of the Earl, of Lathom. The deceased was daughter of Sir Richard. Brooke, sixth baronet, of Norton Priory, Runcorn, and was married in 1832 to the Hon. R. Bootle Wilbraham,. V 7140 predeceased his father, the first Baron Skelmers- da le, in 1844.

div.head: SEVERE FIGHTING IN MOROCCO.
div.p: SEVERE FIGHTING IN MOROCCO.
300 KILLED.

Telegrams from Melilla announce that a great battle • has taken place between the partisans of Maimea Moha- tar and All, the chief of the Mezquita Kabyles, in which, over 300 were killed. The fight was of the fiercest de- sription, and no quarter was given on either side. Whew all the:ammunition had been consumed, the fight be- came a hand-to-hand one. Even women took part by' loadieg muskets and firing dwellings. The village of Frajani was subsequently set on fire, and was in flames. The remnants of Maimoa's party in their flight crossed the Spanish frontier, where some were disarmed and others were driven back into Moorish territory. The fighting V7:1:, then continued. The Sultan's brother re- fused to lend any assistance to the belligerants.

div.head: DOMESTIC TRAUEDY NEAR NUNEATON.
div.p: DOMESTIC TRAUEDY NEAR NUNEATON.

A shocking domestic tragedy occurred on Wednesday morning at Fillingby. Joseph Howard, farmer, aged 64, murdered his wife, Caroline, aged 48, by cutting her throat with a razor, and then committed suicide by cut- ting his own throat. The couple had only been married' three months, but the quarrels between them had been bitter and frequent. Howard called his serving man at 4.30 on Wednesday morning, and about eight o'clock a servant girl, Mabel Wright, in passing her mistress's bedroom, noticed that the bedclothes were stained with blood. She raised an alarm, and Mrs. Howard was found lying dead in the room with her head almost severed from the body. Subsequently Howard was found lying in an adjoining room with his throat cut. He was still grasping a razor. A policeman and Dr. Westwood were summoned, but it was apparent that in each case life was extinct,
