div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, JULY 23, 1892.

MR. GLADSTONE is assured of a " what's to be done ? majority of 4'2 ; and the question arises—" What will he do with it ?" It is not sufficiently large to be what is called a good working majority; and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S prediction is that "the coach will be upset at the first corner." He contends, further, that such a Government as Mr. GLADSTONE may form will be incapable of dealing with " employers' liability, parish Councils, local option, or anything else." It may be that the wish in this case is father tothe thought ; for it is a matter of course to say that, if the member for West Birmingham can manage it, the coach will be upset before it reaches the first corner. Be that as it may, it is the prevailing opinion amongst the Tories and Liberal Unionists that the new Government will not be able to do anything beyond making an abortive at- tempt to get the Home Rule Bill through the House of Lords. The Duke of DEVONSHIRE and Lord SALISBURY have doubtless meant all they said in intlinating that the Lords would throw out the Bill. If Mr. GLADSTONE had at his back a majority of over 100 members, it is not unlikely that the Peers would hesitate about blocking the way; but, as matters stand, they may be counted upon to reject the measure, and force another appeal to the country. And that is what Mr. CHAMBERLAIN means by saying there will be no domestic reform. From the Tory point of view, it would be an astute move to bring about another appeal to the country within the next twelve months; for the cry then would be that Mr. GLAD- STONE was incapable of carrying on the Queen's Government; and the electors, who have had enough of electioneering for a time, might be disposed to listen to the cry. It is hardly likely under such circumstances that the Liberal party would be returned with an increased majority; and the question of Home Rule would be put back for some years.

But what if there should be a now departure in Parliamentary procedure ? If the majority, small though it be, is kept together, each member practically putting himself in the hands of the Whip, it is just poasible that business may be as well got trough as if the majority were a large one. There is this to be remembered— that every Liberal member who has been returned to the new Parliament is definitely pledged to Home Rule ; and, more than this, every member is interested in carrying Home Rille not only because he is pledged but because he may again have to undergo the cost and turmoil of a contested election, if the Liberal majority in the House of Commons is allowed to melt away. But what, it may be asked, is to be done,if the Lords reject the measure? Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S view is that the Irish members will not allow anything else to be done until Home Rule has been carried. But we believe the Irish members will show themselves more rational. Mr. T. P. O'Corirmß, who is more to be relied upon as a spokesman of the Nationa- lists than Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, has already sug- gested that, instead of dissolving Parliament, if the peers reject the Home Rule Bill, the measure

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: should be sent up year after year, the House of Commons proceeding, in the meantime, to carry out the English reforms to which the Liberal party is pledged. It seems to us that this could and should be done, always assuming Mr. GLAD STONE is in a position to keep his majority intact. As Mr. HERBERT GLADSTONE put it, on Saturday night, it is no part of the business of the Liberal party to play into the hands of the enemy; and we gather from his speech that something will be done in addition to trying to carry Home Itule, He said:—

There were things they must do before they weat to the country again. They must bring in a County' Government Bill, which would embody the principle• of local option. The drink question must be settle& both for town and, country. The County Govern— ment Bill must inelude parish councils, and give. powers for the compulsory purchase of land for the purpose of allotments. In the second place there. must be a drastic measure concerning registration, and it must provide that all elections liall be on one day, and for the payment from the rates or con- soliaated fund of the returning officers'. expenses. It must also include the principle of one man ono vote.

It will be seen that this is a view of the situa- tion which is precisely the reverse of that taken by• Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. If the Government could do nothing more than reform the Registration Laws, they would render an incalculable service to the country, fort with the abolition of plural voting, there would be a fair opportunity of getting. at the mind of the nation, and that,. we be- lieve, would mean a return of the Liberals to. power by a majority at least double that which they have secured at the present moment. Ireland,. Scotland and Wales have pronounced strongly in favour of Home Rule and the Newcastle pro-- gramme generally. Abolish plural voting, and it will be found that England, too, will give a majority for the same prcgramine.

The Tan Liberals of the Northwich Northwich Division have not gained a seat by Victory. the return of Mr. BRUNNER, ; yet it cannot be denied that they have gained a victory. There was never any doubt as to Mr. Bainstrina being elected, but it was thought not at all un-, likely that there would be a reduction in the large majority of 1,129 which lie obtained in the bye-election of 188 Z. For one thingr there is always a difficulty in inducing electors to make sacrifice to vote when they are persuaded that their vote will simply swell an already certain majority ; and it is in this way that majorities sometimes vanish altogether. Besides, Mr. George WHITELEY, the Tory candidate, had been for many months hard at work in. the Division. He is a ready speaker, an excellent canvasser, and an experienced electioueerer, backed, to boot, not only by the combined forces of the Tories and Liberal Unionists, but by the long purse of the Duke of WESTMINSTER. To have won under such circumstances, and brought up the majority from 1,129 to 1,255, is an achievement of which the Liberals in the Division have every reason to be proud. Mr. BRU.N,N.ER was somewhat late in the field; he was attending to his duties at West- minster whilst his opponent was addressing the various sections of the constituency ; auct it was thought, at first, that he was letting the Tory candidate have too m.uch of his own way. But Mr. BRUNNER when he did come upon the scene made things lively. His energy and activity were contagious ; they stimulated the workers te such a degree that Mr. WHITELEY'S hopes were speedily dashed to the ground. Still, he fought stoutly to the end and lie was actively supported by men who were altogether unscruplous as to the kind of weapons they used. Libel and slander were to them in the ordinary way of things ; but. their accusations fell from the Liberal candidate like water from a duck's back. I Indeed, in some instances the charges brought against Mr. BRUNNER rather served him. For instance, the statement that "sweating " was Ipractised at Messrs. Brunner, Mood, and Co.'s works brought into prominence the fact that so far is this from being the ease that workmen are now employed eight hours per day only, whilst they are in the happy position of receiving the same wages which they earned when they worked twelve hours per day. ;./Ir. BRUNNER has made money rapidly, but he has spent freely and wisely. It is because he has done this and shown that he is as Liberal in the House of Commons as he is liberal at home that the electors have expressed renewed confidence in him by returning him to St. Stephen's with an increased majority. It is to his credit that he would not listen to the propos ii to have a "walk over " himself, if he would be party to a "walk over" in the Knutsford Division. He believes in fighting for the advancement of Liberal principles ; and recognises that, if the Knutsford Division is to be won, it must be won by educating the electors before, during, and after a Parliamentary contest. Further, he has not hesitated to encounter Mr. WHITELEY as the son-in-law of a 'Blackburn brewer; and pledged to watch over the interests of" the trade." There can be no question that the Liberals have suffered in the boroughs through the publicans having allied them- selves with the Tory party ; and the Tory party have made the most of their oppor- tunity in practising those arts of treating which they understand so well. They have not been able to do this so effectually in catinty con- stituencies, where the licensed houses cover a large area, and are more under observation. Besides, as to the Northwich Division, Mr. BRUNNER, made it known that he was making special arrangements to trace bribery, treating, and personation, and this watchfulness has undoubtedly been a terror to evil-doers. It has thus happened that the contest has been fairly fought as well as hardly fought ;. and that it should have resulted in a majority ef 1,255 is 'sufficient to stamp the Division as safe for Mr. BRUNNSR to the end of his days.

ELECTRIC LIGHTING OF THE ST. HELENS TOWN HALL. On Monday, the work in connection with the electric lighting of the St. Helens Town Hall was completed, and the-Current turned on. There are 339 lights,each one being of 16-candle power. The as- sembly-room is lit with three coronas, arranged one on each of the gas chandeliers, each having forty lights. The council chamber has ten groups of three lights in each, and the new-committee room has five groups of five lights in each. The Free Library, Mayors, suite of apartments. Town-clerks,and other municipal offices, corridors, Sze., are also efficiently lighted. In the engine house there are two of Burnstead and Chandler's patent double cylinder silent engines, which couple direct to Holmes and CO's " Castle" dynamos, each of which produce about 200 light. The switch board shows that there are five separate circuits to the building, so that the whole or part may be lighted at once. Ihe fittings has been put in by Messrs. J. D. F. Andrews and Co., of London, under the superintendence of their electrical engineer Mr. J. D. Bailie. The Mayor of St. Helens (Councillor F. R. D. Nuttall) and Councillor Martin (chairman of tile Town Halt Committee) with Mr. O. J. C. Broom, borough engineer, inspected the work, and pronounced it satisfactory. The cost has been about £1,500. Before Mr. J. Birchall, on Monday, at Widnes Police Court, John Walsh, Widnes, was charged with stealing a jersey suit of clothes, the property of Jabez Unsworth, clothier, Waterloo-road, Widnes.—Helen Waterson de- posed to seeing prisoner take the clothes produced off a nail by Mr. Unsworth's door, on Saturday night. She endeavoured to take them away from him, but failed to do so.—Joseph Bushell, assistant to Mr. Brookes, clothier, corroborated .—P.C. Fisher arrested prisoner and charged him with the offence, when he said "1 was drunk, and did not know what I doing." Prisoner was committed to take his trial at the Liverpool Assizes.

At Widnes Police Court on Tuesday, before Mr. H. Wade Deacon, Bridget Mulligan, of Albion-street, was charged with doing grievous bodily harm to Margaret Johnson, also of Albion-street, by kicking her in such a manner as to break her left leg. The two women had been quarrelling for some days past, and it was alleged that on Monday night the prisoner caught hold of the complainant by the hair of the head, dragged her about, and kicked her with great violence on the legs.—Dr. Hutchinson said complainant's left leg was fractured in three places, and she was unable to appear.—On the application of Superintendent Keighley, prisoner was remanded for a week. JOSEPH PRITCHARD has the best stock of ladles' shyer and gold watehee In the tawn.—Advt. THE POTTERY TRADE AND THE SHIP CANAL.

At the monthly meeting of the North Staffordshire Chamber of Commerce, held on Wednesday afternoon, at the Hanley Town Hall, the only business transacted was the reception of a report from Mr. E. V. Greatbach upon a recent visit of a committee of the chamber to Runcorn docks. The report dealt with the works of the Manchester Ship Canal now in progress in the vicin- ity of Runcorn, and their effect upon the pottery traffic. The President said it would be clear to all that the inter- ests of the district were not being overlooked. The conditions inposed upon lhe Canal Company were being carefully carried out. The altered condition of things at Runcorn had entailed very heavy expenditure upon the Ship Canal Company, and as the concessions made to the Chamber would probably enable the canal to be opened six months earlier than would have been other- wise poss. lilo, the saving would be considerable. They had been ail!, to help the country in this public-spirited manner withoot in the least endangering the Interests of their own district, and they still had the power in their hands in caso any of the conditions imposed upon the Ship Canal Company were not complied with of stopping the works within 24 hours. Mr. Boddington said that when the new order of things got into swing their district would be better off even than it was in the old days of Runcorn, because they would be able to bring up the ships without waiting for the tides at Liverpool. The district by helping the Ship Canal Co. would find in the end that it had done itself a good tu-n.

Early on Thursday morning a terrible death befel a colliery drawer named John Gittins, aged 20, who resided at 10, James-street, Tyldesley. div.head: ST. MICHAEL'S BAZAAR, RUNCORN.
div.p: ST. MICHAEL'S BAZAAR, RUNCORN.

In connection with the recent fête and sale of work on behalf of the chancel fund of St. Michael and All Angels' Church, Runcorn, a balance sheet has just been issued. It shows the receipts to have been—Admissions. £3O 18s 4d. ; Girls' Friendly Society stall, £B5 9s. 6d.; Birdie Wood's stall, £l2 lie. std. ; advertisement stall, £39 9s. 34d. ; flower stall, £l3 12s. ; St. Michael's stall, £ll4 ss. ; Parish Church stall (including donations) , £126 14s. 61d. ; refreshment stall, £33 81. 6d. ; sweet stall, £l9 3s. 6c1.; ente-tsinments, £5 ; donations pqr Rev. G. H. Seeley, £2 12s. ; sale of flower tent, £4 ; total receipts, £487 4s. 21,1. The expenses amounted to £73 14s. 6d., leaving the handsome balance in the bank of £413 9s. Bid. BEAUTIFICATION OF ST. EDWARDS CATHOLIC CHURCH, RUNCORN, Signor A. F. De Cavalier°, of Liverpool, has just com- pleted some further artistic decorations of the Catholic Church, at Runcorn. *The latest docorations consist of representations of St. Patrick and Our Lady, in the Chapels dedicated to the saints named, and the Virgin. They are painted in oils, and the figures are most cleverly executed, while the colours show that besides being the conception of a highly artistic mind, he has a thorough knowledge of the technique of his profession. It will be remembered that Signor Cavallaro recently painted the portrait of Dr. Gastaldi, the respected pastor of the church, in oils,and high encomiums were bestowed upon the work. The ceremony of blessing the decorations was performed on Sunday by the Rev. Father Dunlevy, 01St. Lawrences Church, Birkenhead. ELECTION OF TWO PROCTORS FOR YORK CONVOCATION.

The clergy of the Chester Archdeaconry held a meet- ing in the Cathedral Chapter House on Monday, under the presidency of Yen. Archdeacon tarber, for the pur- pose of electing two proctors for the York Convocation. A letter was read from one of the retiring proctors, the Rev. Canon Cooper, late of Tarporley, and now stationed at Cuckfield, in which having tendered his resignation as proctor, he thanked the clergy for the confidence they had so long reposed in him.—The can- didates proposed were the Res. Canon Dodd (Stretton), retiring proctor • Rev. Canon Maitland Wood (Runcorn) and Rev. W. E. 'Torr (Carlett Park, Eastham). Each candidate was asked several questions, and a show of hands resulted in the Rev. Maitland Wood Nina first, the Rev. W. E. Torr second, and the Rev. Canon Dodd third. A poll was demanded on behalf of Canon Dodd, and forthwith opened, the result of which will be declared in a few days. •

A RUNCORN WILL SUIT. In the Divorce and Probate Division, on Tuesday. the President had before him the case of Watkin v. Whitlow which was a suit for a grant of probate of the contents of a will of Henrietta Hooper, Runcorn, deceased, who had resided at Southport. There was no opposition. Mr. Bayford, Q C., appeared for the plaintiff, an execu- tor of the will, which was dated 4'h December, 1886. He said the estate amounted to £1,700 or £l,BOO, and by the will in question it was divided between the near- est relations. He explained th,it testatrix's mind became affected, and in 1887 she destroyed the box containing the will and all her papers. It was alleged that she was not sane at the time, and she was afterwards confined in an asylum. In proof of her mental condition he men- tioned that she had several times tried to commit suicide. Evidence in support of this having been given Mr. Powles said he appeared for four of the defendants, and they consented to probate. His Lordship granted probate of the copy of the will.
FROSF.CIITIoN UNDF.R TIM FACTORY. ACT AT WIDNES.

Before Mr. T. H. (1 ..4s4g,r arid Mr. F. A. Stapleton Bretherton,at Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, the British Patent Portland Cement Co., carrying on busi- ness in Ditton-road, Widnes, were summoned by Mr. H. S. Richmond Government factory inspector, to answer a charge of contravening the 73rd Section of the Factory and Workshops Acts (1878), by not sending the neces- sary notification ot the existence of their works to the Inspector. Mr. Richmond said the old Company had not notified him, and although this Company had been in occupation since February he had not received any notification from them.—Mr. R. S. Pearson,the secretary to the Company, said the matter had been overlooked. —A fine of 20s. and costs was inflicted. The Company were further summoned under the same Act, for not having certain machinery in the works guarded as re- quired. Mr. Richmond said he visited the works on the 25th June, and he then found one of the engines totally unguarded, and other machinery insufficiently so. This offence was also admitted, and a fine of 40s. and costs was imposed.

EXTRAORDINARY ATTEMPTED SUICIDE AT WIDNIIS.

On Saturday, at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. 11. Wade Deacon, Richard Boyce, 79 years of age, was charged with attempting to commit suicide by drowning himself. P.C. Hargreaves stated that about nine o'clock on Friday night he was told that a man was endeavour- ing to drown himself in a' pond off Norland's-lane, Farn- worth. Be proceeded in the direction indicated, and found the prisoner in a hay field naked, with his clothes, which were wet, lying by his side. Witness asked him what he was doing there, when he replied that he had tried three times to drown himself, but was unable to do so owing to the roots of the trees in the pit. A razor and a pocket knife were found in his pocket. Superin- tendent Keighley said Boyce had attempted to take his life in a similar manner twelve months ago, and was then sent to the workhouse, where he had been detained until a fortnight ago.—ln answer no Mr. Lewin, the prisoner said he felt discontented and thought he had lived long enough. By direction of the magistrate the prisoner was given in charge of the relieving officer and conveyed to the workhouse.

THE ELLESMERE LODGE OF FREEMASONS, RUNCORN. The festival of St. John, in connection with the above lodge, was celebrated on Thursday evening, at the Free- masons' Hall, Runcorn. There was a large number of the members of the lodge present, as well as brethren from the lodges at Fradsham, St. Helens, Widnes, War- rington, and Liverpool. The instsllation of the Wor- shipful Master-Elect for the ensuing year, Bro. C. W. Phillips, P.G. Std., of Daresbury, was effectively per- formed by the retiring W.M. James Littler. Afterwards the newly-installed W.M. invested his officers as fol- lows :—Bro. Jas. Littler, I.P.M. ; Bro. T. Smith Bur- gess, P.G. Std., SW.; Bro. T. Sharrocks, J.W.; Bro. W. R. Wass, P.M., treasurer; Bro. T. H. Annett, P.M., P.G.T., secretary ; Bro. J. Coxhill, P.P.G.A., D. of C., P.M., director of. ceremonies; Bro. W. Hankinson, S.D. • Bro. A. Linaker, J.D. ; Bro. A. Salkeld, 1.G.; Bro. W. E. Lancaster, organist; Bro. J. Le Couteur, almoner; and Bro. T. Lydiate, tyler. After the despatch of the Masonic business, the lodge was closed by the W.M. in due and solemn form. The brethren then sat ,1 down 00 sumptuous banquet in the ante-room, under the presidency of the Worshipful Master. Subsequently the loyal and masonic toasts were honoured,interspersed 1 with songs by Bros. Phillips, Littler, Cooper, Branch, and others. TREAT TO DUTTON WORKHOUSE CHILDREN._

The fourth annual visit of the Dutton workhouse children to the seaside took place on Tuesday, when about fifty were taken for a day's outing to Southport. The party were under the guidance of the master and matron, Mr. and Mrs. Cunnah, assisted by the school- master (Mr. Naylor), and the schoolmistress (Mrs. Nut- tall), and were accompanied by the chaplain, the Rev. L. D. Lyon Bennett, and party, and Mr. H. E. Heywood and Mr. Williams, Guardians for Frodsham. The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, chairman of the House Committee,met the children at Southport. The weather was wet and boisterous in the early part of the day. It had been in- tended to take the little folks on the marine lakes and to give them unlimited fun in donkey riding on the sands, but, after a brief visit to the new lake, this part of the programme had to be omitted. A move was then made for the Centenary Exhibition, and on arriving, the general manager (Mr. Spier) at once kindly offered to admit the children free to Professor Jennion's marvel- lous marionettes, which were heartily enjoyed, after which the unique collection of art treasures was in- spected, and, with other special attractions, the after- noon passed very pleasantly. A walk through the town and selecting toys for the sick and little ones at home brought tea-time round. The return journey was com- menced soon after seven o'clock, and Dutton was safely reached about nine. Mr. Williams distributed sweets and gingerbread to the children during the day, and Mr. Wright, of Halton, sent buns to the station in the morn- ing, and thanks are due to Mr. Shaw, of Liverpool, for the two through carriages and the privilege of travelling at night by the Crewe express, which was allowed to stop at Preston Brook. The funds had been provided by the Guardians, ex-officio Guardians, and a few friends. HOUSEHOLD LINENS hemmed and marked free of charge during sale at J. and W. DUTTON'S. Sankey-at., Warringto

An Oldham correspondent states that the Execu- tive Council of the Federation of Master Cotton Spinners at a meeting of cotton spinners, on Tues- day, came to the conclusion that a reduction of 10 per cent, in wages, and the running of the mills short time were necessary to afford relief to em- ployers in the present depressed state of business ; and it was also resolved to call a special meeting of the Federation to further consider the matter. It is stated thatshould an attempt be made to give effect to the views of the Council a great strike is certain to take place. On Monday morning, Martin Fenna, the Irishman charged with feloniously stabbing Thomas Jones, landlord of the Nag's Head Hotel, Farndon, on the eve of the Rddisbury election, was brought before the Btoxton magistrates. Dr. Thelwall stated that prosecutor could not attend, owing to the serious nature of the scalp wound. The knife, coming in contact with the skull, had glanced a couple of inches downwards, causing a great loss of blood.— Prisoner, who belongs to County Clare, said he drew the knife in self-defence.—The prisoner was re- manded.

THE COAL TRADE OF SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE. Thek .have been rumours throughout St. Helens and Haylock that a reduction in miners' wages would pro 'ably be made on account of the slack- ness of trade but we are informed on good autho- rity that no se lh reduction is contemplated, and the St. Helens iners' agent (Mr. (Hover) has heard nothing of it. He says it would hardly be at- tempted in a small district, as the federation could successfully resist any such action. A resident in Haydock on Monday stated that ,there has been more "play" during the past twelve mouths than during any previous period since Haydock was started as a mining district. This would apply to ordinary periods and not to strike periods.

FATAL TRAP ACCIDENT AT LOWTON.

- -- An accident, which terminated fatally, occurred shortly after seven o'clock on Sunday evening in what is known as Mather-lane, Lowton. It appears that about the time named a number of children were playing in the road near to where they lived when a phaeton driven by Mr. Alfred Calland, of Market-zt., Leigh, and a trap driven by Mr. James Pendlebury, also of Leigh, came dashing up at full speed. The children at once made to the roadside, but one of them, named Elizabeth Houghton, aged one year and seven months, was nnable to do so. Several people who were passing at the time cried out to Calland to stop, but as the other trap was attempting to pass him he does not appear to have realised what they were calling for, as the next instant the child was caught by the front wheel of the vehicle and its head almost split in two. Drs. Dobb and Sephton were at once called in and at- tended the child, which suffered until five o'clock on Monday morning, when it passed away, never having regained consciousness. ROYAL MANCHESTER, LIVERPOOL AND NORTH LAN CASHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.

From an announcement appearing in our adver- tising columns, it will be seen that Thursday next, the 28th instant, is the opening day of the above Society's Great Show at Newsham Park, Liverpool, and that it extends over Monday, the Bank Holiday. The Show, we believe, will be one of the most important ever held under the auspices of the Society, and will no doubt be a source of great at- traction both to agriculturists and the public gener- ally. The total number of entries considerably exceeds that of any of the Society's previous Shows. It is gratifying to find that the importance .of this Society's show meeting is vastly increasing, and that this year the Liverpool Show may well rank as second only to the Royal of England. The main entrance to the Show is off Shell Road, and there is aa entrance at the other end of Gardner's Drive for the convenience of visitors from Stanley Railway Station and that direction. Given suitable weather, there is no doubt the Liverpool meeting will be a pre-eminent success. Crieketing Goacis.—GARLAND, Sporti' Warehouse, War- rington.

SUPPOSED DROWNING OP A COLLIER. During the early part of the week, the police, and the friends of a collier named Richard Jackson, of Porter's Cottages, HaVdock, have been engaged in dragging operations in the Sankey canal, and the brook adjoining, for the body of the man Jackson, but so far without success. It appears Jackson, with another collier named Peter Hughes, also of Porter's Cottages, Haydock, left the Ship Inn, on the canal bank at Earlestown, about eleven o'clock on Friday night. The men seem to have been under the influence of drink, as, after crossing the canal by the bridge, they lay down on the grass between the canal and the brook and fell asleep. Hughes awoke about one o'clock on Saturday morning, and endeavoured to arouse Jackson, but failing to do so, he left him asleep and went home. Jackson never made an appearance, and his friends have seen nothing of him since. The mark of a clog was found just on the edge of the brook and opposite to , where he was sleeping, and it is supposed that on awaking he has walked into the brook and been drowned. The heavy rains have greatly swelled 1 the brook, and his body, if the supposition be cor- rect, may have been carried away some distance from where he is supposed to have fallen in.
Mr. Joseph Oxton, farmer, Storetem, near Birkenhead, fell into a pit of water on his farm, on Wednesday, and was drowned.

The Heywood Unionists have abandoned the intention of petitioning against the return of Alderman Snane. The South-Western Railway dividend for the past half-year will be at the rate of 41 per cent, per annum.

, . Two men at Abercarne colliery were buried by the fall of about forty tons of roof, and were not discovered for four hours. Both weie frightfully mangled, and one can hardly survive.

div.head: THINGS HEARD ANT) SEEN AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THINGS HEARD ANT) SEEN AT RUNCORN.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

At last the election is over, and the victory was as decisive as the most enthusiastic supporter of Mr. Gladstone could possibly wish for. The fiklit has been a very keen one, and everybody would have been glad had the day of decision been a week earlier, but there was no altering of the fiat of the returning officer.

The poll was a very heavy one, being over 85 per cent, of the electorate. There were 810 more votes recorded than in 1887, and of these Mr. Brunner ob- tained 468 and Mr. Whiteley 342. It was the confi- dent prediction of the Tories that if Mr. Whiteley did not win, he would at least greatly reduce the majority, and it was freq.iently predicted that Mr. Brunner would not be in by more than 100. But he has not only more than held his own with the new voters, but he has increased his majority to 1,255

The organisation of the Liberals was exceedingly. complete. In every district, besides the sub-agent there was a band of voluntary workers who have during the past few weeks been working incessantly, and who on the day of the poll displayed an energy and ability that augured well for the result. Speak- ing of Runcorn alone, Mr. W. Carroll, chairman of Runcorn North,and Mr. John Clark,chairman of Run- corn South, are deserving of all credit for the efforts they put forth, and the same may be said of all their assistants,but it is impossible to particularise. A high compliment was paid to the organisation of the party by Mr. Causton, M.P„ who went round thevommittee rooms on Monday, and he told Mr. Handley that had they such an arrangement of affairs in the metropolis they could win the whole of London. Coming from a gentleman who has been a reformer in these matters, this is a high compliment indeed.

It has been exceedingly gratifying to a larae number of Liberals to see Mr. P. Speakman, C.C., taking such an active part in the contest. He has not only taken the chair at several of the meetings but he has worked in other ways and his help has been of the greatest value.

-- Runcorn has usually been considered a stronghold of the Liberal party, but now we are told that Mr. Brunner's majority was obtained in Northwich District, and that Runcorn did not give hitu a majorit) of more than 100 if any a:, all. If this is so why all these murmurs of dissatisfaction that one cannot pass through the street without hearing,and which are aimed against a gentleman whom they ought to thank under such circumstances?

The action of the returning office, Mr. Cullimore in appointing only two local solicitors, and the rest gentlemen from Chester, to officiate in the seven polling booths there were at Runcorn, has met with considerable condemnation. Such a thing has not been done previously and it is justly con- sidered that the local gentlemen of the robe have.a claim to such positions. I have heard that one of these gentlemen was so well acquainted with registration and electioneering that he allowed a man to vote fore starred number. It would thus appear that some of these gentlemen were not chosen for their special fitness for the office, and the Runcorn lawyers have a grievance.

Now that the contest is at an end, we can once more settle down to the ordinary affairs of life, and meet our friends without entering into discussions on the personal merits of the candidates or the wis- dom or otherwise of Home Rule. And any bitter- ness of feeling that may have been engendered in the course of the battle, ought to be forgiven and forgotten.

Bye the bye out of the 9905 votes recorded there were only 25 spoiled papers. Eleven were marked , with writing, three were double marked and eleven were blank, the latter evidently not intending to vote for one side or the ether. This exceedingly small number of spoiled papers speaks well for the general intelligence of the electorate. 411.1.

div.head: DAVIES TESTIMONIAL FEND
div.p: THE DAVIES TESTIMONIAL FEND

A meeting of the members of Runcorn Football Club, with the object of considering the best means of raising the testimonial fund for the widow and children of the late Mr. T. LI. Davies, formerly a prominent member of the first team. Mr. P. Speak- man C.C., presided and there was a very numerous attendance.—The Secretary relyl letters from the president of Cheshire Football Association .(Mr. Thorpe), from the secretary of that Association,and the secretaries of New Brighton, Biricenhead Park, West Lancashire Rugby Union, Stockport, and Warring- ton football club;. A donation of £5 was enclosed in the Warrington letter. The writers all conveye4 their deep regret at the great loss the club had sustained by the death of Mr. Davies and expressed sympathy with the bereaved ones. The writers also promised to do everything they possibly could to further the testimon- ial fund on receiving information of what it was in- tended to do. The Chairman said the loss sustained by the club had been to him a very painful experience. He paid an eloquent tribute to the good qualities of the deceased member ; and referred to the respect to his memory paid by the townspeople when his remains were committed to the grave. He wished them to show their sympathy for the widow and two children in a practical manner, as they were totally unprovided for. He and the secretary had taken an early opportunity of inaugurating a teitimonial fund, and he was glad to think that the result was that the family would not he in any way neglected. Mr. Davies was trusted and beloved by all of them, and when the subject was taken up by such a noble army as he saw around him he felt sure that a large amount could be obtained.—A letter was read from Mr. Jesse Timmins enclosing a cheque for a guinea, being his own subscription and that of Mr. F. A. Lightburn.—The Secretary narrated the proceedings so far,and they were approved by the meeting. He also announced that the subscription list had been headed bv Mr. Speakman with a donation of £5. It was decided that the fund be place ll in the names of time president (Mr. Speakman), Mr. Longshaw, the secretary, and Messrs. Harry Wright and W. Faulkner. It was further resolved that a memorial stone should be erected to the memory of the deceased out of the funds of the Football Club. The secretary was instructed to write to the various clubs with which Runcorn had been connected asking them if they would kindly give a gate towards the fund. A vote of thanks wa.s accorded to the the Rev. J. Handley for the beautiful address he delieTered at the graveside.

div.head: PEN KETB.
div.p: PEN KETB.
TINNING COMPANY'S TRIP.

On Saturday last the employes of the Penketh Tanning Company had their annual trip. The des- tination was Southport. The morning was very wet, but a very fair number assembled. The train left Sankey station at 9.30. The day turned out fine afterwards, and a most enjoyable time was passed in the various places of amusement. The party arrived home about 10.30. SANKEY PAROCHIAL TRIP.

The annual parochial trip in connection with St. Mary's Church, and Mission Room, took place on Monday. The place chosen this year was Llandud- no A large 'bus started from the Crown Inn, at six o'clock and another from Sankey church. Both 'buses were well filled. The party proceeded to Bank Quay station and took train to Llandudno. The journey was much enjoyed. Home was reached about 10 p.m. Mr. W. Skelton and Mr. J. Milling- ton, churchwardens, had charge of the arrange- ments. TESTIMONIAL TO TIIE REV. T. E. WINDER.

Mr. Richard Boardman, sexton of St. Mary's Church, Sankey, has exhibited in his window, an illuminated address to the Rev. T. E. Winder, late curate of St. Mary's Church. The address should have been presented to him prior to his departure, but unfortunately, it was not completed. It runs as follows :—"To the Rev. Thomas Edward Winder. We, members of the congregations worshipping at .St. Mary's Church, Great Sankey, and the l'enketh Mission Church, tende7 our sincere regret at your departure from amongst us. We desire to record the earnestness of your labours whilst curate of this parish, and to express our high appreciation of the same. As a slight remembrance of the regard we entertain for you, we ask your acceptance of this address, together with a study desk and table. Whilst regretting your departure, we are pleased to hear of your professional advancement, and pray that God may give you health and happiness in your new sphere." Signed, E. S. Jackson, vicar; W. Skelton, and James Millington, churchwardens, and several of the congregation.

Further cholera riots have occurred in the province of Saratoff. which is discribed as having been given over to mob violence during the past three days. The workmen in the Sunderland shipbuilding yards have received notice of a reduction in wages varying from five to ten per cent. The Court of Session at Edinburgh has authorized a recount of the votes of the Greenock election.

div.head: TEMPERANCE MEETING AT RUNCORN.
div.p: TEMPERANCE MEETING AT RUNCORN.

Last evening week a temperance demonstration was held at the Salvation Army Barracks,Runcorn. Mrs. E. Wynne Humphreys presided, and was sup- ported by a large number Of ladies and gentlemen, amongst them being Mrs. Ormiston Chant,the Revs. Canon Hicks (Manchester), W. Arrowsmith, A. Finch, J. Hanby, J. Pulford Williams, and J. S Simpson; Messrs. E. Wynne Humphreys, A. R. Norman, D. Bisbrown, T. Cooke, W. Mundin, E. Mar-hall, and J. W. Boyle, &c. Mrs. Humphreys said she was very pleased to meet her co-workers in the grand cause of temperance': The work of temperance reform was many-sided, and until they saw that, that they would make very little head- way. A great deal might be done by moral suasion,but she thought something might be done to aid the cause , by the Imperial Parliament. That meeting was not a political one, for if it had been,they would not have had their friend Canon Hicks on that platform. (Applause.) Mr. Humphreys read a letter of regret for his inability to be present from the Rev. Charles Garrett.

The Rev. Canon Hicks, who met with an enthusiastic reception, said he came there as a temperance worker, as a clergyman of the Church of England, and as a friend of all causes which enabled them to do anything on behalf of their great country. (Applause.) He did not stand there as a politician. The work would not progress unless there WAS moral and spiritual suasion, but temperance reform vras' launched upon the great troubled sea of English party politics, and its success would depend upon their sacrifices, and upon them carrying out their convictions. Now that almost every man had the franchise, the danger was that men would vote without thought, or perhaps would not vote at all ; but every man who did that betrayed a very great responsibility. (Applause.) They not only wanted sober working-men, but also sober working women and from various statistics it appeared that the curse was spreading with terrible rapidity amongst women. What could they do in God's name, and in the name of their great country, to help forward this cause ? They must lessen the temptation of drunkenness. Alt they asked from Parliament was to allow them to try the experiment to do without a drink shop—not all over the kingdona,but simply where the inhabitants desired it. That was the Direct Veto Bill in a nutshell. Everyone in a certain district must be asked, and the decision arrived at by the majority of the population, and then, at the end of the year, when the licensing session was held,the magis- trates could not say what houses should be licensed, but whether the people wanted any or not. (Applause.) He believed the time was ripe for wholesale legislation in the cause of temperance, and he urged upon those pre- sent to vote for the candidate who would pledge him- self to support the direct veto—be he Unionist or Liberal.

Mrs. Ormiston Chant, in an earnest and pathetic address, depicted the terrible results of the drink traffic in the country. Speaking of the compensation clauses, the speaker said it would not be the publican who would benefit by the Act, but the large brewers. Dealing with local option, she said they wanted the temptations lessened, and that was the object of the Bill. The meeting was brought to a termination by Canon Hicks pronouncing the Doxology.

BLAKE LEES CHAPEL, KINOSLEY.—The annual services on behalf of the Sunday School were held on Sunday afternoon and evening,the preacher being Mr. J.Buckled. There were nice selections of hymns at each service, and the singing was much enjoyed. The collections amountey to £l4 35. for the day. CHURCH-ST. SUNDAY SCHOOL9.—On Wednesday the aanual treat to the Misses Crostield's Sunday school acholars took place, when they were conveyed by train to Warrington, and from thence in omnibuses to Wal- ton Lea, the residence of Mr. John Crosfield, where a thoroughly enjoyable day was spent. The party arrived at Frodsham station about 8.30 p.m.

• MARRIAGE OF MISS WALKER —On Monday afternoon, at Milnsbridge, Huddersfield, the marriage ceremony was celebrated of Mr. Joshua Shaw, of Fallowfield, Manchester, to Miss Mary Mary Eliza Walker, daughter of Mr. S. Walker, stationer, &c., Frodsham, by the Rev. Alber H. Walker, of Huddersfield, the brother of the bride. The wedding presents were of a choice character. PRIMITIVE METHODIST SCINDLLY SCHOOL.—The anniver- sary services in connection with this school were held on Sunday, the sermons being preached by the Rev. .T. G. Bonsan, of Hyde, morning and evening. In the afternoon a children's service was held, at which recita- tions and songs by the scholars and choir were given ; also an address by the Rey. J. G. Bonsan. This service was ably conducted by Mr. J. M. Jones, of Frodsham. Tne anthems and special hymns were nicely rendered by the choir, accompanied by the organ and a small band of stringed instruments. The offertories for the ' day realized the handsome sum of £2O Os. id. Finn IN A RICK-YARD.—Ahnut four o'clock on Wednes- day afternoon, a haystack in the rick-vard of Mr. Wm. Ellison, Claim Farm, Kingswood, was discovered to be on fire. News was conveyed to Frodsham, and thence a telegram was sent for the Runcorn Fire Brigade, a number of the members of which, with Superintendent Wright, turned out with the engine. They journeyed with speed, reaching the spot about seven o'clock. On their arrival they found that their services were not required, those engagA by Mr. Ellison, assisted by labourers from adjacent farms, having succeeded in extinguishing the outbreak, and in saving a portion of the hay. The loss is covered by insurance.

Patrick Doran, was on Wednesday. sentenced at Down Assizes,to ten years' penal servitude for the manslaughter of Felix M'Mahon near Banbridge. The death was announced on Tuesday of Mr. Thomas Cook, originator of the famous excursion agency which hears his name. Mr. Cook, who is 84 years of age, was latterly blind, and the cause of death was paralysis. The Executive Committee of the Liberation Society have passed a resolution expressing great satisfaction at the return of a Parliamentary majority committed to the policy of disestablishment, and the increased number of members who are favourable to disestablishment: A house in the suburbs of Richmond, Virginia, has been struck by lightning, and a man, his wife, and three children killed. At Brickhead, Georgia, a school for coloured children was set on fire by lightning, and two children were killed in the stampede which ensued.

div.head: AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: AT WARRINGTON.
THINGS HEAIZ D AND SEEN

We have it on a cei tail' authority that the police- man's lot is not a happy one. But it is sweetened with the prospect of a pretty substantial pension after a lengthened period of service. But then, again, it isn't every policeman who gets a pension, and especially, I should say, it isn't every Warring- ton policeman. I believe there is only one retired constable who, at Ow present time, is geLting bene- fit from the superannuation fund connected with the police force. One might argue from this,seeing that the local police force comprises some 53 men, that the odds against a Warrington policeman ever getting a pension are at least fifty to one. As all the men contribute 24 per cent, of their wages to- wards the superannuation fund, it seems rather hard that so few of them should ever have reaped any benefit from that fund.

Church of England clergymen don't depend al- together upon endowments, nor yet upon the con- tributkons of the faithful. There are other little sources of income, which are not to be disdained, seeing that, generally speaking, " the smallest contributions are thankfully received." For in- stance,in the annual report of the borough treasurer, I find, in the cemetery accounts that the sum of £199 7s. was paid as church burial fees. This sum was allocated as follows :—the Parish Church, £B4 10s. 6d. ; St. Paul's, £45 4s. 1041. ; St. James's, £l2 19s. ; St. Anne's, £29 6s. ;.Holy Trinity, £l9 Bs.; and St. Barnabas's,XB 56. Bd.

A curious circumstance occurred on Sunday, afternoon, at the Warrington cemetery. The coffin containing the remains of a man named Henry Allen, a blacksmith, were about to be committed to the grave, when it was discovered to be too small, and the mournful proceedings had to be delayed about ten minutes, while it was being enlarged. I have not heard whether the undertaker or the sex- ton was responsible for this hitch, but certainly it is always deplorable that anything of this descrip- tion should. mar the impressiveness of the last offices to the dead.

I was surprised that the Rev..). T.Wardle Stafford, in his lecture at Sankey Bridges new Wesleyan School, on Monday night, on '' Robert Moffat, or Africa's debt to Warrington," should have omitted to mention the one fact which most closely connects him with this town. As is well known,the building in Bank-street, Buttermarket-street, was formerly a Wesleyan Chapel, and Robert Moffat was at one time in the habit oi attending it. It is strange that Mr. Stafford should not have mentioned this interest- ing item in the biography of the cerebrated mission- ary.

Speaking about Moffat, I must say that while I dmire the heroism and the objects of such men I confess I cannot thoroughly understand what Emerson calls "this incredible tenderness for black folk a thousand miles off." I cannot help thinking of the heathen at home, the "heathen of Warring- ton " of whom Mr. Guest, as Mr. Stafford's chairman, spokeon Monday night; and asking myself whether some of the enterprise and the money devoted to the reclamation of the uncivilised Africans might not be better utilised in reclaiming those at home from the evils of our own at present far from per- fect civilisation.

• -- Our police court this week furnishes an example of the necessity of missionaries in our own immedi- ete midst. Brutality and savagery are rampant in Warrington, and in many other parts of England to-day: though happily we have not reached the condition of things prevailing in America, where negroes are burnt alive by white men, and white men are massacred by those of their own race for not being trades unionists. Pondering on the pre- sent and the past, one is often inclined to doubt whether we have so much occasion to pity the savages as we suppose.

A number of Warrington Liberals have, been anxiously looking forward to having an opportu- nity of congratulating Mr. Gladstone as he passed through the town on his way home from his trium- phant campaign, but through there being no an- nouncement as to when he would leave Scotland, have been disappointed. The right hon. gentle- man passed through Warrington on Thursday night, reaching Bank Quay Station at 11 26. Ile travelled in a saloon carriage which was connected with the mail train, and in which thTre were with him Mrs. and Miss Gladstone and Mr. Armitstead. There was nobody on the platform at the time ex- cept the porters and about half-a-dozen postmen. The latter gave Mr. Gladstone a salute, and he opened the window, and he and his wife and daughter waved their hands in response. The carriage was coupled on to the Chester train and he left Warrington exactly at 11.32 The hale old veteran of Liberalism appeared to be asleep as he entered the station. lam only sorry that the name of Warrington as called out by the porters would not sound so politically melodious in his ears as could have been desired. But the flowing tide, let us hope, will yet in due time overflow thepier point. MERLIN.

div.head: WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.

Last evening a well-attended meeting of the Council of the above Association was held at the Liberal Club, the chair being occupied by Mr. W. Piernoint, Chairman of the Executive. Considerable discussion took place as to the late election, and the future prospects of the party,a strong opinion being expressed that the struggle for Liberalism must continue in the borough until its principles were triumphant at the poll. The following resolution, moved by Mr. S. Wright and seconded by Mr. W. Roberts, was unanimously adopted : "That this meeting of the Liberal Council hereby expresses ita unabated confidence in the leaders of the Liberal party in Warrington, and more especially in the Chairman of the Executive, and hopes that he, in company with others, will continue to lead the party until it succeeds in returning a Liberal Mem- ber for Warrington." The proceedings concluded with the usual votes of thanks. .

div.head: BEFORE THE NIA.GIISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE NIA.GIISTRATES.
A RUFFIANLY WIFS BHATIM,

Michael Mannion, collier, from near Preston, who had been lodging with his wife Bridget, at Hill-st., was charged, at the Warringtoa Borough Police Court, on Monday, with being drunk and assaulting her at their lodgings, early on Sunday morning. It appeared from the woman's and other evidence that soon after twelve p.m. the prisoner and his wife were in their bedroom and he commenced to accuse her of being " thick " with his brother, and to taunt her on this subject. She .told him he was in a strange house, and if he made .any more bother he would get locked up, whereupon he began to use her most shamefully, beating her on the breast, and back, kicking her violently over the body, knocking her down and giving her a black eye, also tearing off her chemise and leaving her on the floor with nothing upon her. He bad been in the habit of abusing her; and at the County Sessions had got three months for assaulting her. Harriet Dainteth heard the woman's screams and she and John Hines ran up and burst the door open, and found her lying on the floor bleeding from the nose and lying on the floor with no clothes on, while the prisoner was standing over her, drunk, and beating her. They called in P.C.Rylatt who took the prisoner into custody.—The prisoner said when he went to bed on Sunday morning he found his wife lying on the bedroom floor, and lifted her into bed. As soon as he got in she seized hold of him and tore his shirt, and " scratted " him in his fate. He had had a drop of drink, and gave her a bit of a shove, but never struck her.—Alderman Harrison, who was on the Bench : And you expect us to believe that 2—The prisoner : I should be believed as well as some of them. She was in the abit of getting drunk, She was drunk the same night.-T-Inspector Spinks : She was sober.—The Chairman (Alderman Francomb) : It is only last month you were let off to take care of her be- cause we thought she would be in such a lonely condition. Your fair glMaicie; won't always carry you through. Six months' imprisonment.

Oe Pasitrsts rod tißtAWildt PttaPo3/1, Patriek Kilroy and Michael Curley, were chargsa be. fore the Warrington Sorough magistrates on Monday morning, with being found on the premises of Mr. Toft at half-past 12 that morning with ; intent to commit a felony.—lnspector Spinks deposed that he heard a noise proceeding from the entrance at the back of Mr. Coates's, leading from Friar's Green, and where Mr. Toft had built some new premises, with a wall about nine feet high. He got P.C. Anson and some other constables, and they surrounded the place and caught the prisoners. They foand them in the warehouse not asleep, and had some difficulty in getting them out over the high wall. —Kilroy said he and Curley only-went to have a sleep. —P.C. Amson corroborated the Inspector's evidence, stating that the men were sitting in the store room.— Mr. Toft said there was property about the place that might be stolen, but no one but these men had aver made entry in this way .—Curlev said;he and Kilroy had just come out of Strangeways Jail, and went into the premises for shelter so as not to get locked up again. They admitted that it was drink that had brought them to their present condition.—They were dismissed with a caution.

- ---.--. THREE MANCHESTER BOY ADVENTURERS. At the Warrington Borough Police Court en Tuesday, George Downey, James Johnson, and John Simms, all boys, from Manchester, whose addresses there had been ascertained, were charged with unlawfully offer- ing in pledge at Mr. Hmghton's pawnbroker's, in Mersey-st., a lady's diamond ring, and George Downey was charged with stealing the ring. It appeared that they had offered the ring for IBs., but Mr. Houghton, jun., being suspicious, called the attention of the police to th 6 prisoners, and they were taken into custody. Johnson then said the ring belonged to a young woman at his father's house in Manchester, his brother having bought it for her.—The Chief Constable read a telegram he had received from a Mr. George Harris,of Manchester, on Monday afternoon stating that three boys had ab- sconded from there the previous afternoon, but remarked that this did not appear to refer to the prisoners.—They were ordered to be handed over to the custody of the Manchester police.

MR. DIGGLE AND HIS TENANT. Mr. William Diggle, at the Warrington Police Court, yesterday, charged Joseph Poulter with fraudulently removing his goods from a house belonging to the com- plainant at 5, Pierpoint-st., to avoid distraint for £3 175. ed., rent 17 days in arrears.—Mr. Diggle said on the 11th just he called at the house and told Mrs. Poulter that he should be obliged to distrain if the amount were not paid, and subsequently found that the defendant had removed the goods. The defendant's wife wished to explain, but was not allowed to do so, the cass being adjourned a week for Mr. Diggle to bring a witness to the removal of the goods.

THEFT BY LADS FROM A CRICRET FIELD. At the Warrington borough police court yesterday, William Smith, son of Edward Smith, 22, Dale-street, Sankey, and James Murray, son of Thomas Murray, 1.43, Dale-street, Sankey, both aged 11 years, were chargdd with stealing two cricket bats, two sets of stumps, two pairs of legs guards, a pair of gloves, and two balls, value £2 65., the property of the Wesleyan Zion Cricket Club at Sankey.—The Chief-constable said the articles were locked up in the pavilion between 8 and 9 o'clock on the previous Tuesday night, and on the Wednesday towards noon, it was found that it had been broken . into and the articles carried away. Mr. Alfred Bailey, cap- tain of the club, in consequence of what some children told him, went to the field adjoining the cricket field and under the grass found some bats and other things. On Thursday night he reported the matter to P.C. Chrimes, and on Thursday about midnight the lads were appre- hended at their homes by D. S. Monaghan and Inspector Spinks. They at first denied all knowledge of the articles, but Murray ultimately said there was a pair of loves under some bricks in his father's back yard. The officers found them there, and Murray said the other things were in a grass field, and there the other articles were found.—Mr. Bailey said a hat and two pair of leg guards were not recovered .—The lads were ordered to be kept in custody till 6 o'clock and be punished with six strokes of the birch rod each.

Ax IMPUDENT Tnvarr.—John Jefferies, a young man, was charged with being on enclosed prem isos in Orford- street for an unlawful purpose, and also with stealing 45., the money of Henry Jenks, at the Theatre Tavern, Scotland-road, on Friday evening.—Henry Jenks stated that he was a mill furnace-man at Dallam Forge, and lived at 10, John-street. On Friday night he went into the vaults of the Theatre Tavern, about a quarter to eleven, and called for a glass of beer. He also bought some tobacco, and the prisoner, who was in the vaults, asked him to give him a "pipe." Witness told him he must buy his own tobacco, as he had to work for his. The prisoner came up to him and took two 2s. pieces out of his waistcoat pocket. He asked him to return the money, but he took no notice of him. He jostled up against him, and he (prosecutor) afterwards found his watch hanging from his waistcoat pocket. He pushed the prisoner away from him, and a struggle ensued. They eventually got outside,and witness told the prisoner he would give him in charge. Prisoner punched him in the mouth , and witness gut him down, and shouted " Police " two or three times. A man with a crutch came up and parted them, and prisoner went away. He never got his money back, and he was quite sure the prisoner was the man who took it from his pocket. George Lunt, manager of the Theatre Tavern, said he ejected the prisoner and the complain- ant from the vaults. Further evidence was given to show that the prisoner was found en the premises of Henry Gittins. stone-mason, Orford-st., about one o'clock on Saturday morning. He was asleep on the boiler. He was brought to the Police Station by P.C. Amson, and afterwards identified by the prosecutor as the man who had robbed him. When taken into cus- tody prisoner had only 20. in his possession. In reply to one of the constables, who said prisoner was only "act- ing sleep," prisoner exclaimed, "I don't know ; you hit me very hard to waken me." (Laughter.)—Prisoner (crying) protested that he was as innocent of the charge as a new-born babe.—The Bench committed him to pri- son for a month's hard labour.

ALLEGED THEFT or Boors.—Geerge Harris was charged on remand with having in his possession a pair of men's boots, and not being able to give a satisfactory account of them. P.C. Booth, of the Cheshire police, gave evi- dence to the effect that the owner of the boots had been found in Runcorn. Prisoner was handed over to the Cheshire police.
MONDAY.—Before Aldermen.FrancOmb (chairman) and
Harrison.

DRUNK AND DISOIIDERLT.—WiIIiain Lythgoe, on Satur- day night, in Battersby-lane, ss.- and costs.—John Connor, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Bridge Foot, also with assaulting P.C. Clough on Saturday night, after his ejection of him from the Packet House Inn. 10s. and costs.—James Loftus, at Bridge Foot the same night, ss.—Henry Beech, in Buttermarket-st., that night, ss.—Patrick Gorden, in Dallam-lane on Saturday night, dismissed with a caution. —Patrick Crawley and Michael Heavy in Buttermarket- st. that night, ss.—Thomas Reed, in Cockhedge-lane on Sunday morning, 3s. 6d.—Henry Mather in Buttermar- ket-st„ on Sunday night, Ss. and costs. DBUNK.—Mary Jeffreys, charged with being drunk in Winwick-st. on Saturday night, was dismissed. DRUNK AND RgFITSING TO QUlT.—Patrick Kelly. for being drunk and refusing to quit the White Bear Inn, Buttermarket-at., on Saturday night, 103. Tr OF Boois.—Stephen Collins was charged with stealing on Saturday afternoon, a pair of child's boots, from the shop of Valentine Morton, St. Jarnes's•street. He pretended to be looking for something for another man taking the opportunity to carry off the boots, which his wife afterwards pledged at Mr. Houghton's. The man was apprehended by Sergeant Cheney. He said it was drink that had caused him to commit the theft, and if the magistrates would let hicn off he would goj straight to the chapel and take the pledge.—The Bench sentenced him to two months' imprisonment with hard labour, and advised him to tako the pledge when he came out. _

PrrcH AND Toss. Arthur Lomax, aged 17, son of Thomas Lomax, 17, Crossley-street; John Allen, aged 13, 21, Crossley.street, and WilliamWolstenholme, aged 15, son of William Wolstenholme,of the Manx Arms, School Brow was charged with playing at pitch and toss in the neighbourhood of School Brow on Monday. Mr. A. Browne defended Wolstenholme.—P.C. Clough having given evidence against the lads, Mr. Browne stated that they were not on public ground as stated, but on private land, belonging to Dr. Cannell. He also called Wolsitenholme's father and three other witnesses, whose evidence went to show that there had been no tossing, and that the boy Woistenhohne was in his father's bar at the time in question.—The Bench dismissed the case as a doubtful one.

FffirmNo.—Joseph Warburton, a cripple, for fighting on Tanners' Brow, on the 9th inst., was cautioned, but dismissed. STREET OBSTRUCTION.—Joseph Matthews for allowing a quantity of refuse to stand at the back of Chorley's marine stores, on the 6th and the 12th inst., was fined 2s. 61. in each case. Tagsnar.—Before Mr. E. J. Guest. .

SLEEPING IN A HAYSTACE.—JARISS Graves, who said he came from Birmingham, was charged with being found sleeping the previous night, in a haystack belonging to James Robinson, off Winwick-road, and with doing damage thereto to the amount of 6d. The constable who proved the case said the man had Is. 2d., a pipe, tobacco, and matches on him, and Mr. Robinson proved the damage. Ths prisoner was fined 2s. 6d., including costs, in default seven days. AN UNSEEMLY Womasi.—Norah Butler,married woman, was charged with unseemly behaviour in Sankey-st., soon after midnight that morning. She asserted that she had.on leaving her husband,been dogged by men,and in order to get out of their way took shelter in a house and got over the back wall, to get away from them,but was waylaid by them. Her husband, she said, played a violin and sometimes a concertina in the streets. The , Chief Constable said he had a report of a violin and bow being missing, and about a woman also disappear- ing, but did not know whether the prisoner was the woman.—The constable gave further evidence, from which it appeared that the advances of a man with whom the prisoner was caught were not forced upon her as she stated, but willingly accepted. The can was dismissed.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Holmes (chairman) and Wright. __ __ .

C RUB LT T TO Ho RS —F;ederick Golboddy, horse dealer, from Manchester, was charged with being drunk and cruelly beating two horses in Winwick-street on Tuesday. D.S. Monaghan proved the case and said pieces of the stick the defendant beat the animal with were flying in all directions. The defendant was fined 20s. and costs.—Henry Burt was charged with cruelly beating a horse in the same street on the same day.—lnspectors Dowty and Wilson, R.S.P.C.A., proved the case, Mr. Dowty saying that the defendant gave three different addresses. He was fined 10s, and costs. Hugh Grant, for maltreating a horse by cruelly beating it in Tanner's. lane, on fuesday night, was fined 10s. and costs.

AN ABSENTEE MILITIAMAN. Clement Webb was charged with being a deserter from the 3rd South Lanca- shire Militia since June sth. He was also said to be Pleficient of about eleven articles of clothing and neces- saries.—Ele was fined 40s. and casts ; in default 14 days. TRURSDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton (chairman) and Captain Ridgway. DRUNK AND AMAULTING CONSTABLES.—MichaeI Callag- han w.ns charged with being drunk and disorderly in Queen-st.,the previous night, and with assaulting P.C.'s Hardy and Amson. P.C. Hardy said the defendant was drunk and creating a disturbance on the Fair Ground at about twenty minutes to twelve on Wednesday night,and refused to go away. Witness and P.C. Amson took him into custccly, and opposite Stubbs's works, in Scotland- road, he kicked Hardy several times and struck Amson. He acted like a madman all the way to the Staticn.— He was sent to prison for a month. FRlDAY.—Before Aldermen Harrison (chairman), and Wright. UNLAWFULLY PLEDGING A Rody, aa Irishman, was brought up on remand charged with un- lawfully pledging a gold ring with George Jackson, pawnbroker, on the 18th inst., without being able to give a satisfactory account of the same.—Mr. Jackson said the prisoner told him the ring had been given to him, and afterwards that he found it at Chester.—D.S. Monaghan said the prisoner told him he found the ring at Chester, and afterwards that he picked up on a rail- way platform between Chester and Warrington, a box containing the ring and another found on him.—He was bound over in £lO to appear again if called upon, the Chief Constable retaining the rings. CRUELTY TO A FlORSE.—William Wood was charged with cruelly treating a horse by working it while in an unfit state on the 13th inst., in Buttermarket-st., and George Wood was charged with allowing it to be so worked.—Enspector Dowty. R.S.P.C.A., and P.C. 17„ stated that there was a large wound under the saddle' which was pressing on it.—The defendant called a witness, who said the saddle was tvesi inches off the plaster that was on the wound.—The defendants were fined 10s. and cots each. A DEFAULTING APPRENTICE.—Benjamin Ogden was summoned by Edmund Mills, fustian cutter, as surety for his daughter,for recovery of Bs., claimed as com- pensation for her absence from work.—The defendant said he had understood the amount would be stopped off the girl, but offered to pay it in sums of 2s. per week.—The complainant accepted the offer,and the case was adjourned eight weeks to see whether the amount was paid. MORE WOMEN'S QUARRELS.—POLITICAL FEELING AGAIN. —Catherine Bolton, 105 Bostock-st., was charged with assaulting Elite, Dutton, on the 18th inst. The com- plainant sad she passed the defendant's door as she was standing there and merely asked her to chastise her little girl for striking her sister, upon which the defend- ant said " I will chastise thee," and struck her on the mouth filling it with blood, then brought out a tin of water and threw over her.—Corroborative evidence wasl given.—The defendant said the complainant lifted her ' umbreFa to her and said " I will stick it down your throat," and she warded it off, and in doing so hit Mrs. Dutton in the mouth.-1 boy named Savage said Dut- ton was " ran-tanning" on Mrs. Bolton's door with a big stick. Other evidence was given for the defence, and Bolton was bound over iu £5 to keep the peace for six months, and mulcted in costs.—Mary Glynn, 4 Ship- yard, was charged with assaulting Fanny Thompson,

, . Nzutecr or FAMILY.—Alfred Birchall, labourer, was charged with leaving his wife and family chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union, on the 6th July. Mr.S. Shearer stated that the prisoner's wife and two children were admitted to the workhouse on the 6th July. Every inquiry was made with a view to finding the prisoner, but withdut success. The Guardians allowed the prisoner a week to turn up, and as he failed to do so, a warrant was issued for his apprehension, and the police found him in the town. Two of the pri- soner's children were admitted in December last, and they had really four of his children in the workhouse. His family had cost the Union about £l6. The Guar- dians were obliged to take some steps because the union schools were full, and the children were chiefly those who had been deserted. The prisoner's family were ab- solutely starved when they took them in. It was stated that the prisoner earned about 183. or 19s. a week.— Re was sent for a month's hard labour.

6 Ship-yard, on the 19th inst.—The complainant said she had come from a wedding and she was wearing s blue ribbon, and the defendant said" What are you wearing that colour for ?" and struck her with a scrub- bing brush.—ln reply to the Chairman, the complainant said she was not wearing the ribbain as a political demonstration, but she expected the defendant thought she was.—The defendant said the complainant had aggravated her by calling her an Irish cow and other approbrious names.—Glynn was bound over in £.5 te keep the peace six months, and had to pay 9s. costs.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Major Pickmere (chairman) ami Mr. James Tinsley.

DiFoLccr OF FAMILY.-Mr. B. -Shearer, prosecuted William Webber, on behalf of the Warrington Guar- dians for leaving his wife and three children chargeable to the Union. Mr. Shearer said the defendant had worked in the tan yard at Penketh, and earned 321. to 353. per week, but, as he had admitted, had lost his situ- ation through drink. P.C. 657 said the defendant had been discharged five or six times from the tannery for drinking.—The defendant said he had only been dis- charged from it once.—He was sent to prison for a month's hard labour.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Martin Churchill, James Ramsdale, and Samuel Jones, drunk and disorderly at Burtonwood on the Bth inst. were fined ss. and costs.— John Perrin, basket maker, Thomas PQmberton, farm labourer, and George Taylor, greengrocer, were charged with being drunk and disorderly at Rixton on the 6th inst.—Mr. Browne defended.—P.C. Schofield said the men had a barrowful of cabbages on the footpath and were throwing them about and making a great noise. They had been drinking all last week and during this week. He never threatened to report them for not having hawkers' licenses.—P.C. 1079 corroborated, and said he asked the men if they had hawkers' licenses. —The defendants swore that they were sober at the time, and Taylor said Mr. Hayes had given him the cabbages to sell in the village, as he was going to start as a greengrocer in his shop, which he had since done. The constables never charged them with drunkenness, but with not having licenses.—Mr. Hayes deposed that he saw the defendants soon after perfectly sober.-ss. and costs each. _ _ _
CYCLING ON THE FOOTPATH.—David Budge, for this offence, atGreat Sankey, on the Thursday previous, was fined is. • __. .

ASSAULT ON A BEERROUSE REEPER.—Wm. Davies, was charged with assaulting James Hayes, beerhouse keeper, at Great Sankey, on the 18th inst. The complainant said the defendant refused to pay for four glasses of beer that had been ordered, and witness took them away upon which Jones followed him into the kitchen and struck him twice. 10s, and costs. _

BREACH OF THE INFECTIOUS DISEASES ACT.—Thomas Cottam, of Croft, was charged with failing to report on the 23rd inst. the fact that his horse was suffeling from glanders. The defendant said he thought the animal had only a cold.—The animal had been destroyed by order of Mr. Hewitt, veterinary surgeon. Cottain was fined £1 and costs.

BOAT ACCIDENTS- OFF SHETLAND.
LOSS OF SIX LIVES.

A boating accident occurred in Yell Sound, Shetland, on Wednesday. by which four persons lost their lives. Mr. Robert Williamson (late of the Ship Hotel, Leith). his wife, his brother John, and a Eqherman named Alexander Gray were in a sailing-boat, when it capsized, and all were thrown into the water and drowned, no assistance being possible. Mr. Williamson was a native of Yell, and was paying a visit to his friends. On Sun- day, a similar accident occurred in the same Sound, by which as old man named Green and a boy lost their lives.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

It is not often that a player is fortunate enough to secure the whole of Ids opponents' wickets in a cricket match. Such an incident, however, occurred on Satur- day at North Leeds, Crosthwaite for the hne team capturing the whole of the Yeadon wickets for 53 runs.

Although Dr. W. G. Grace has done almost everything possible in cricket Shrowsbury's performances of late are almost without precedent. He has scored 420 runs in a fortnight in six innings (twice not out), so that so far this month he has an average of 105 runs. With innings of 151 and 11, each time not out, in the Gentlemen v. Players match, and 116 against Yorkshire, he has an average of 278 for the week !

Dr. Gilbert Grace was unfortunately not able to res- pond to the invitation of the Surrey Club to take part in the return match between the Gentlomen and Players. He first played for the Amateurs in 1885 at the request of the Surrey Executive. Excepting in 1867, 1883, and 1892, Mr. Grace has taken part in both matches ever since 1865. Since 1865 Mr. Grace has played 90 com- pleted innings for the Gentlemen against the Players. He has scored 3,652 runs, which gives him the solid and and substantial average of 40.57. At Lord's he has scored 134 not out in 1868, 109 in 1870, 112 in 1872, 163 in 1873, 152 in 1875, and 169 in 1876. At the Oval he has compiled 215 in 1870, 117 in 1872, 158 in 1873, and 100 in 1881. At the old Prince's Ground in 1874 he contributed 110, at Brighton in 1871 217, and at Hast- ings in 1891 169. Thus it will be seen that in 1870,1872 and 1873 he ran into three figures in each encounter.

The two great rival counties of Notts and Yorkshire have not had the satisfaction of beating or being beaten by each other, for both matches ended in draws, and thus don't count. It was extremely hard lines for Notts in last Saturday's game, for they had it well in hand when the rain put an end to the proceedings. Although Notts have done so well this year, and are pretty certain of the championship, the attendance at Trent Bridge has not improved, and even with such a draw as York- shire not more than 5,000 put in an appearance during Thursday and Friday.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

W. Townley, the International footballer, connected with the Blackburn Rovers has left and signed for Stock- ton, who now have a very fair team indeed. Rowdier, who cost the Rovers £25 last season for an imaginary interview, has now been transferred by the Wolver- hampton Wanderers, and will fill Townley's place very well.

As the result of complaints of non-fulfilled engagements made by Lancashire clubs against Yorkshire clubs, joint action will probably be taken by the football committees of both counties. The complaints have arisen owing to engagements in Lancashire being prevented from fulfil- ment by the Yorkshire Cup ties. As the dates of the Cup ties are always known beforehand, it should be an easy matter to so arrange fixtures as to prevent clashing, but when a club goes further into the Cup competitions than it has bargained for, compensation for unfulfilled fixtures is at any rate a reasonable proposal.

Matters in connection with the Rugby League for Lancashire are said .to be progressing favourably. So kindly have the authorities looked upon the scheme that it is said the County Committee contemplate taking the thing in hand themselves, and by giving the full weight of their influence and power to the projected idea to make it the great success which the promoters prognos- ticate. By thus showing their sympathy with the players and a desire to help the League, they will un- doubtedly make the new scheme representative of the strength of the County, while if the plan is comprehen- sive its attractiveness will be as certain as its success.

The honour of leading the bowling averages this week belongs to Attewell, who holds the premier place with an average of 13.05, Watson retires to the thira position, but the greatest change is seen in the advance which Mold has accomplished by his splendid bowling against Kent and Middlesex, and his figures are now 1390 against 18.11 last week. Briggs also shows im- proved form, though not quite so marked as his county companion. Lockwood and Lohaman hold the sec3nd and fourth positions respectively, with decimals over 13 for each wicket while Wainwright and Peel in com- parison with others have receded a little. J. T. Hearne is still the hardest worked bowler of the list, having sent down no less than 951.2 overs for an aver- age of 16.06.
