There were numerous athletic sports in connection with clubs within easy distance of Warrington on Satur- day,and the local men who entered for the prizes offered came off with fair success. At the Salford Harriers, E. Osborne, from the 10 yards mark, was third in the 120 yards handicap. J. Yates, Salford Harriers, was first from the 8 yards, A. W. Ware' of the same club, with Ti yards start, taking second prize. H. Webster, of Warrington with 13 yards start, was first in the 440 yards hurdle race. Rochdale Infirmary Gala gave Rabbit, of Warrington, a chance of showing his sprint- ing powers, and this he creditably did by capturing the first prize in the 440 yards handicap. At the same sports W. Leatherbarrow, of the Warrington Cycling Club, was third in the three miles bicycle handicap. Leatherbarrow had 50 yards start, Rabbit being con- ceded 35. J. Buxton, of the Warrington C.O , was third in the one mile bicycle handicap at Salford Harriers Sports, from the 160 yards mark. The winner was J. Parry, Liverpool, who was conceded 155 yards start.

div.head: SHIP CANAL AND CHANNEL TUNNEL FOR IRELAND.
div.p: A SHIP CANAL AND CHANNEL TUNNEL FOR IRELAND.

LETTER FROM SIR E. WATKIN, Sir E. Viratkin, M.P., in a letter to the " Times,' sugghsts that the Irish question should be settled by the joint action of Liberals and Conservatives, and adds :—One great thing they could settle—a question more important to Ireland, as it seems to me, than a dozen Home Rule Bills—a question which can be discussed quite apart from Home Rule controv- ersies. It mean the restoration of prosperity and pro- gress by great, but simple, public Works—the leading works being (1) a ship canal of capacious dimensions between the west and east of Ireland, and (2) a tunnel from the North of Ireland to the South of Scotland. The former would place Ireland on the shortest sea road to all the great West, and to the East, via the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the latter would make Ireland and Scotland one country. Surveys and disscussions to which I and others have for years been parties have demonstrated the feasibility of both projects, and the most liberal estimate for both does not excead £20,000,000, which at three per cent, ninety-nine years' terminable security would amount to a burden of £600,000 a year for ninety-nine years, or about a fifth of the cost of keeping a hostile force in Ireland. I have gone with others into the financial part of these ques- tions, and I believe each of these works would pay, and ' the United Kingdom would gain and not lose by the investment. I shall be happy to show to anyone the plans and sections of a canal across Ireland prepared for me under the charge of the late Mr. T. A. Walser, who constructed the Severn Tunnel and most of the Manches- ter Ship Canal; and as repects the tunnel, I refer your readers to the discussion at the Society of Arts in Febru- ary, 1891, the Duke of Abercorn in the chair.

div.head: NET LIBERAL GAIN
div.p: NET LIBERAL GAIN
LIBERAL MAJORITY.

The results of the final polls of the present general election, which were declared on Tuesday, have finally determined the issue. It was thought that the Liberal majority might possibly be increased by the gain of one or two more seats, both the Handsworth Division of Staffordshire and the High Peak Division of Derbyshire being looked upon as exceedingly " shaky" in their allegiance to the Uniopist cause. Both, however, have returned members of the same colour as before. These were the last seats in which a win was possible to the Liberal party, the remainder of the outstanding polls having been represented in the last Parliament exclu- sively by Liberals or Nationalists, and had no further change taken place the Liberal majority would have re- mained at 44, the figure at which it stood after the Liberal victory in West Denbighshire was declared on Monday. But the Lichfield division of Staffordshire, by the extremely narrow majority of 4, the smallest but one declared in the present contest, has ousted Sir John Swinburne, Bart., the late Liberal member, and • elected Major Darwin, who stood as Liberal Unionist. The Unionist gains are thus raised to 26, which, deducted from the Liberal gain of 81, leaves a net Liberal gain of 55, and reduces the Liberal majority to 42. The only constituency now remaining unpolled is Orkney and Shetland, the election in which takes place on the 25th and 26th inst. The latter is regarded as a safe seat for the Liberal, so that there is now no pros- pector any farther alteration in the relative strength of parties.

FIGHTING IN AFGHANISTAN.
REPORTED DEFEAT AND SLAUGHTER OF THE AMEER'S TROOPS.

SIMLA, WEDNESDAY.—The HUMS are reported to have twice entrapped the Ameer's troops into an am- bush, killing many hundredti of hem and capturing a large number of Mies and ammunition. A Waziri raid has occurred in the Zhob Valley, near the Gomel Pass, and three men of the Tribunal Levy were killed. It is be- lieved that the raid was the result of Afghan influence. The Ameer. has nlw replied to the representations recently addressed to him by the Government of India, expressing concern at the progress of events in Bajaur and warning him that no attack was to be made on Umra Khan. His Highness's letter states that he will not attack Bajaur without provocation, and throws the blame of the recentcollision entirely upon Umra Khan.

div.head: QUEEN'S VISIT TO OSBORNE.
div.p: THE QUEEN'S VISIT TO OSBORNE.

The Queesi left Windsor for Osborne on Tuesday. The Clarence Yard,Oosport, was reached at half-past twelve. The ships in harbour were dressed with flags and the Royal Standard was flying from the public buildings. On alighting the Queen was received by the Naval Com- mander-In-Chief (the Earl of Clanwilliam) and the General Commanding (the Duke of Connaught) with their suites. The Duke of York was also present. Her Majesty and suite embarked on the Alberta (Staff-Capt. Goldsmith), which was lying alongside, and the yacht cast off in a stiff breeze and rainy weather just before one o'clock. There were no salutes. The yacht crossed to the Trinity Pier, East Cowes wbence the Queen drove to Csborne.

Princess Christian and the younger children of Prince and Princess Henry of Battenberg went with the Queen to Osborne. The Queen Is expected to reside in the Isle of Wight till about the 23rd of August, when the Court goes to Scotland, her Majesty being usually at Balmoral upon the 26th of August, the birthday of the late Prince Consort.

Prince and Princess Henry of Battenberg and Prince Alexander left Windsor for the continent immediately after the Queen left for Osborne. They go later on to Bayreuth, as already announcod in "The Daily News.''

div.head: VOLUNTEERS AT BISLEY.
div.p: THE VOLUNTEERS AT BISLEY.

, --- St. Helens is represented by 19 men at the meet- ing of the National Rifle Association, at Bisley, which opened last week, 17 being members of the 2nd V. 8., South Lancashire Regiment, while the 2nd L.V., R.E. have this year for the-first time sent two men. The representatives of the 3rid V.8.,5.L.R are Lieutenant White,Armourer Sergeant F. J. West Sergeants C. C. Wilson, Dwerryhouse and George Junor ; Corporals R. Norbury, Forster, W. J. Milli- gan, and George, Taylor, and Privates R. McGill, D. Gamble, Forsyth W. K. Glover, T. Roberts, T. Nor- bury, R. Preston, and T. A. Lockie. The represen- tatives of the 2nd L.V., RE., are Captain John Roth. well, and Sergeant G. J. Litherland. The members of the 2nd V.B. South Lancashire Regiment, have been entered by the corps for the Queen's and St. George's compatitions, and they have also entered several other competitions. Last week was devoted to general com- petitions, which have hitherto been shot for during the Queen's week, these including the Albert, and several minor competitions. Saturday, however, was a big day The competition for the possession of the Elcho Chal- lenge Shield was very keen, and it was finally won by the Scotch team with, the grand total of 1696, against England's total of 1692 and Ireland's total of 1665. The shooting for the Kalspnre Cup was commenced early in the afternoon, and in this competition there were teams representing the mother country,Canada, Guernsey, and Jersey. At the conclusion of the contest it was found that the mother country had again won the trophy with a total score of 684, against Canada's 662, Guernsey's 659, and Jersey's 656. There were several other competi- tions during the afternoon. Thirty-six county teams have competed for the China Challenge Cup, and the London R. B. team are the probable winners with 383 points.

div.head: RUMOURED DESTRUCTION OF AN ISLAND. 12,000 THOUSAND LIVES LOST.
div.p: RUMOURED DESTRUCTION OF AN ISLAND. 12,000 THOUSAND LIVES LOST.

SYDNEY. MONDAY.—News has arrived of the occurrence of an almost incredible disaster at Sangir Island, which lies midway between Mindanao, the most southerly of the Philippine islands, and the most northerly point of Celebes. According to the statement of the captain of the steamer Catterhun, belonging to the Eastern and Australian Shipping Company, which has just arrived here from China and Japan, he called in at Timor Island on the 19th ult. There he found a Dutch steamer, the master of which stated he left Sangir, which is the largest of the Talautse group of islands, on the 7th ult. A few hours later a terrible explosion occurred, showers of ashes descending on the deck of the steamer, and the whole of the surrounding atmosphere being darkened. When the clouds of debris and dust at last cleared away nothing was visible upon the horizon but clouds of vapour, which extended for many miles. Nothing could be seen of the island of Sangir, which prior to the erup- tion had been full in sight, and the Dutch captain expressed himself as firmly convinced, that the whole island had been blown to pieces, and the entire popula- tion, estimated at 12,000 souls, had perished in the eruption. He added that there were ix sailing vessels at the island when his steamer left, and that these must also have been destroyed. When asked by the captain of the Catterhun why he did not return to the spot to assure himself of the truth of his impression, the Dutch captain stated that the sulphurous condition of the atmosphere compelled him to get away as rapidly as possible. The captain of the Catterhun further states that the large island of Luzon, in the Phillippine group, had recently suffered severely from volcanic eruption's, which had set fire to and devastated a large portion of the island. Nineteen days after the reported catastrophe at Sangir he passed Celebes, the shores of which were strewn with deoris.

div.head: EARL OF ORKNEY MARRIES AN
div.p: THE EARL OF ORKNEY MARRIES AN
ACTRESS.

On fuesday at All Souls' Church, London, Miss Connie Gilchrist, the well-known burlesque actress, was married to the Earl of Orkney. The approaching union had been kept a secret, but about a hundred people were in the church, though there was a conspicuous absence of members of the theatrical profession, whilst the Duke of Beaufort was almost the sole representative of the bridegroom's own erder. Miss Gilchrist was accom- panied to the altar by the Duke of Beaufort. The Rev. W. P. Legge, senior curate of All Souls, performed the ceremony, at the conclusion of which Lord and Lady Orkney, accompanied by the rest of the party, proceeded to the vestry, where they subscribed their names to the register. The bridegroom's signature was (Edward Walter) Orkney, and the bride's Constanc. Macdonald Gilchrist. The signatures of the witnesses to the marri- age numbered seven, amongst them being the Duke of Beaufort, Gillie Farquhar, and the respective solicitors of the contracting parties. The wedding breakfast, to which about a dozen guests were invited, afterwards took place at the bride's residence in Duchess Place. The bewly wedded pair subsequently left for Exeter en route for Minshead, where the honeymoon is to be spent. " And who is Miss Connie Gilchrist, I pray ?" asked the Lord Chief Justice, in his most silvery tones, and with the blandest of smiles (and the" Pall Mall Gazette" puts the same question). The question was put to a leading counsel in the court over which Lord Coleridge presides ; and the occasion was a cause célèbre which, for the regulation nine days, occupied the public mind. Then—it was several years ago, of course—Miss Gilchrist was a popular Gaiety actress ; on Tuesday she became Lady Orkney. The incident recalls Miss Lavinia Fenton, the Polly Peachum of the "Beggar's Opera," who so suecessfully sang and danced herself into the affections of the Duke of Bolton more than a century and a half ago. A more recent precedent for the Earl of Orkney's conduct will be found in the case of the Earl of Clancarty whose countess was once the delight of the motley music hall crowd. The Right Hon. Edmund Walter Orkney, of the parish of All Saints' Wing, in the county of Buck- ingham," a " bachelor of the age of twenty-one years and upwards," put in his appearance recently at Doctors'-commons, and " prayed " for a licence which would enable him to become married to Constance Macdonald Gilchrist, " a spinster of the age of twenty- one years and upwards ;" and the licence was, upon payment of the usual fees, duly granted. Everybody— except, of course, Lord Coleridge—knows Miss Gilchrist. She was for years the " bright particular star" of the Gaiety stage. But she left the stage when Mr. Hollings- head gave up the Gaiety management ; and since then has resided in Duchess-street, Portland-place, and at Melton Mowbray. She is said to a Diana among hunters. and has regularly accompanied the hounds for a good many seasons past.

div.head: Letter. to the (traitor.
div.p: Letter. to the (traitor.

NUISANCES IN WARRI.NGTON.—A COMPLAINT. Sir,—ln most communities in this country the Nuisance Inspector is the paid servant of the Local Authorties elected to that office by the ratepayers. Having occasion to request the attendance of the Nuisance Inspector, Mr. Ralph Norman, with regard to a nuisance that is being perpetrated in the neighbour- hood of the Dial Mills, we were surprised te learn that he was not paid for his services, by the ratepayers, but as he very graphically put it " He paid for him- self." Now, sir, if this is the way affairs are conducted in this community we venture to think that the sooner a change is made in this direction the better. We have a duly appointed Health Officer, whose duty it is to examine and inquire into all nuisances of every de,scriptien whatever. On the 11th of May, 1892, We addressed a letter to the Chairman of the Health Com- mittee in respect to a very serious nuisance, to which we have had no reply. Now we are told by the Inspector himself that it is not his duty to reply to com- plaints ; and neither is it his duty to examine into a com- plaint after one o'clock in the afternoon on Saturdays. As ratepayers we are entitled to have our complaints attended to,and if impossible to remedy them, at any rate, cause should be shown why such should not be done. When we appeal to the Chairman of the Health Com- mittee and no notice is taken of our letter, and we request the attendance of the Nuisance Inspector and I are told by that official it is not his business to reply to such letters. We have no other alternative except to ask ) u •-) give publicity to this letter, with a view of ascertaining if possible, why we are in such a peculiar a position, and, if it is the custom here in Warrington to treat all ratepayers in this manner; or, as new corners, if it is not thought necessary in our case, to pay any attention to our complaints.—We are, yours respectfully, W. A. BISHOP & CO. ' Dial Mills, Warrington, 21st July, 1892.

div.head: SOME LIBERAL CONSOLATIONS.
div.p: SOME LIBERAL CONSOLATIONS.

Sir,—Though the Liberals of Warrington, and the im- mediate neighbourhood have been defeated, they have not been disgraced. They made a gallant fight fir a good cause, and, though worsted, can look on it, if not with- out regret, at least without remorse. This applies only to those who fulfilled their pledges. Those who did not —who knowingly and deliberately perjured themselves are not worthy of the name of men—they are political

vermin. My own observation goes to prove the truth of the saying that in this contest the Liberals were the sober party. This should be a consolation to all right- thinking Liberals. Again, I am glad to say, that I saw none of those meretricious mendacities so prevalent on the other side —none of those appeals to our lower nature—to our unreasoning prejudices. For instance, I should like to ask was Mr. Legh responsible for that pictorial mendac- ity that figured so largely on his voting card ? By the way is it typical of the Tory estimate of history to as- sociate the names of Blake and Drake Ste. with the union which did not take place before the beginning of the present century ? I am glad to say that this pictured lie—the torn standard—failed to pervert the Eccles division: It was tried here along with the mean statement that Mr. Roby's company had estab- lished a branch of their works in France. It is a con- solation to Liberals to know that for them this kind of dirty work is unnecessary—for them, argument and principle suffice. Another great consolation is to be found in the fact that even when Liberals fail to get a Government of their own way of thinking—the party in power is compelled by the Liberal public opinion of the county to bring in and pass Liberal measures ad- vocated and agitated for by their opponents. So the Liberals, even when not in the shafts, have the privilege of driving the donkey. Locally the Liberals of Warrington have this consola- tion, that if they failed to get a Liberal representative— the change is a distinct gain to the constituency. Yours &c., JOHN PEERS. Penketh, July 17. th, 1892.

WARRINGTON ELECTION. Sir,—The Warrington election is over, and has ended, as many people expected; more the pity. An oppor- tunity has been offered Warrington of redeeming its lost character, but it has not availed itself of the chance. "500 votes for 500 pints of beer," is a stigma not easily wiped off ; it will take at least a generation to remove

that blot. Where else than Warrington would you see a Bung Manifesto like the production that disgraced the walls and aardings of the town last week ? " The shriek for" liberty" and the yell against " tyranny and teetotallers," if it were not for its hypocrisy and wicked- ness, would be amusing; as it it, it is contemptible. According to Bung,it is tyranny to rescue those who have, fallen into his clutches, and to prevent others from be- coming the victims of his thraldom; sobriety is tyranny and abstinence from strong drink slavery ; and all and sundry are warned by the Bung proclamation to avoid teetotallers and tyranny. Warrington needs purging,butt how can it be done? We have a gin dealer for Mayor. The late member was a brewer on a large scale—he well represented the Tories as the silent member, with his one v)te for compensation to publicans ; and these men ars magistrates who make and sell drink! Can they, will' they, put down drunkenness, and by so doing diminish their income? In the nature of things it is not likely. The police are powerless. They state, and truly, that certain houses should be put down and the license re- fused. The licensing magistrates take no hotice of the representation ; the vile dens go on with the work of demoralisation ; and your alderman says your drink. seller must have " fair play." Parties are summoned for drunkenness and discharged because they were not sufficiently far gone. In Warrington drunkenness is rampant, and to put it down would interfere with the interests of " the trade." I write this as explanatory of the conduct of a great many individuals on the election day—who were evidently under the influence of Bung. Mrs. Houston, in passing through the streets of Warrington, was hooted and insulted by men, women and children, and by one at least, who from his position in a public Government office, should have shown better nehaviour. I have understood that the chief had issued a prohibition to Post Office officials to be on their behaviour and to be neutral at election times. I shall write to the chief of the departnumt for his opinion, giving him the name of the party. Dr. Houston, too, in passing Bank QUay, was assailed with opprobious language by a set of viragoes who incited the children to pelt him with mud, I one of them flaunting an old red rag of a flag in hi face. I A similar thing occurred among the" flat " population at Sankey Bridges. They have splendid voices for yell- ing, and they gaVe the candidates a specimen of their

throat power. Warrington is detnoralised by drink—and Bung yells for " liberty." A sober intelligent statesman must not „seek to represent Warrington during the present genera- tion. lie may with Dante write on its portals—" Let all who enter here subandon hope." Still, I think, in the interval, much may be done for its reclamation. I have made, I believe, a few converts to Liberal and just prin- ciples of some who were, or supposed they were, Tories, by reasoning with and showing then calmly and dispas- sionately the two systems. litany people take their poli- tics second-hand, Cr ready made, and believe what they are told ; they are led into error and are content therewith. Let us rouse and rescue them. the Liberal record of the past is one of justice—Liberty, Equality. Fraternity— these are our watchwords for the future as in the past : Where is the wrong ?—I am, sir, yours respectfully, CYMRO. Sankey Bridges, ffulyltith, 189E4 • ,:.• MR. THE EXA-MINER, SATURDAY. JULY 23. 1892.
MR. J. T. BRUNNER, M.P.

Above 16 a portrait of Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., again the chosen Parliamentary representative of he Northwich Division of Cheshire. lle first com- menced his Parliamentary career when the redis- tribution of seats in 1883 carved Cheshire into a number of constituencies, of which the Salt District and Runcorn formed one, and since he was selected by the Liberal Association to fight the battle of Liberalism he has been thrice elected and once rejected. The election which has just been brought to such a triumphant conclusion has mace his seat exceedingly secure, and it is doubtful if the opposite party will again contest the division against him. Mr. Whiteley declared on his entrance into the.district that he had come to fight a forlorn hope, and verily the result has proved the truth of the assertion.

Mr. Brunner has been the architect of his own fortunes. He is the son of a Swiss schoolmaster who had settled in Liverpool, and is now about 47 years of age. In his early manhood he occupied a position behind the desk in the office of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co., Chemical Manufacturers, Widnes, and he ultimately became cashier. At this time Mr. Mond was employed as chemist at the same works, and twenty-two years ago they com- menced business at Winnington as manufacturers of alkali. The young firm did not at once spring into fame and fortune. As Mr. Brunner has often des- cribed, everything appeared to go wrong with them. Everything that could smash did smash, and every- thing that could explode did explode; and it was only the exercise of perseverance, and business aptitude of a high onler that brought the firm from the verge of ruin to a most magnificent success. About 11 years ago the concern was converted into a limited liability Company, with £lO ordinary shares, and a number of preference shares on which seven per cent, was guaranteed. The two partners took up the bulk of the shares. Mr. Brunner is Chairman of the Company, and his personality so pervades all the operations that the works are widely spoken of as " Bruuner's works." The company has been remarkably successful. The bal- ance- sheet for the half year ended Dec. 31st last
al:
JOST

shows a profit of £241,778, which with a balance of £12,150 brought forward, enabled the directors to pay a dividend of 50 per cent, on the ordinary capi- tal. This, too, after placing £50,000 to the reserve fund, and carrying forward a balance of X 36,000. During the last ten years, the works have been extended time alter time, and they cover a very large urea of ground ; and Brunner, Mond, and Co. are always described as the largest manu- facturers of alkali in the world. There are at least 3,000 men and boys employed there, and, as the highest wages in the trade are paid, the weekly wages bill must be a very large one. But, be=ides being well paid,the workmen are well treated in many other respects. Mr. Biunner was one of the first employers to adopt the eight hours system The men work in shifts,and for eight hours' work they receive the same wages as they formerly had for twelve hours. And still there is no falling off in the profits of the firm. Every man employed by the firm, who has a good record for keeping proper hours, gets a week's holiday every year and receives his wages. A strong believer in trades unions, Mr. Brunner has privately and publicly urged upon his workmen to join organisations of that kind, one reason being that it is easier to understand what the men want when their desires are formulated by the officials of a union. The "Compensation for Subsidence Bill," which was recently passed by the Rouse of Commons, was practically Mr. Brunner's measure, and he advocated it most strenuously, although he himself will probably be one of the greatest loser financially. It has been charged against Mr. Brunner during the election that he was not an Englishman. But those who know him best describe him as a thorough " John Bull :" such indeed is the descrip- tion of Mr. Snape, M.P., and there can be no doubt that his sympathies are thoroughly English. He is a great believer in education of every description, and he is a very liberal supporter of educational institutions. His gift of a Free Library to North- wich was an act that will live in the memory of the people there for all time. In conclusion it should be said that Mr. Brunner is a Radical of the most pronounced type, and al- though he may not perhaps be a very fluent speaker, he possesses a political knowledge seldom surpassed, and his speeches as a rule are brimful of fact and sound argument. Mr. Brunner has two residences —one Winnington Old hail, which formerly be- longed to Lord Stanley, of Alderly, and the other at Druid's Cross.

div.head: G-LADSTONE'S RETURN.
div.p: G-LADSTONE'S RETURN.
SPEECH AT KIRKMICHAEL.
ATTITUDE OF THE LIBERAL UNIONISTS.

Mr. Gladstone, accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone, Miss Gladstone, Lord Acton, Mr. Arrnitstead, and Mr. J. B. Balfour, M.P., arrived at Fisher's Hotel, Pit!ochry, from Braemar, on Wednesday evening, a little before six o'clock. The party left Braemar about nine o'clock on Thursday morning, driving by Spittal of Glenshee, where the horses were changed, and the journey was resumed by Kirkmichael, Strathtammel. The party arrived at Kirkmichael about 3.30 p.m., when Mr. Gladstone was presented with two addresses —one from the Liberals of Kirkmichael and district, the other from Blairgowrie and Rattray Liberal Associa- tion. A large crowd had gathered round the hotel door, and the right hon. gentleman was received with great cheering. Mr. Gladstone appeared to be in the best of spirits. The addresses having been presented, Mr. Gladstone, rising in the carriage, replied as fol- lows :—Gentlethen,—lam greatly gratified to find that in this beautiful though thinly-peopled portion of the country so large a number of friends have gathered to greet me on my way; and as - -.thought fit kindly to present me with two addr_ . it is my duty, though I did consider that my pi speaking was Sus- pended for a period—(laughter). insider it my duty to say to you a few words at tin 3t interesting and important juncture in the nati de ies. (Hear, hear.) Gentlemen, I rejoice to both these , thougw 'v are local iming from ively
1 where th '.4tlmed

whict _ justly - and honourably expres.... (Cheers.) We all feel, gentlemen, that the Irish question is our question, and until we make an attempt to settle—nay, more, until we make a successful attempt to settle the Irish question, Ido nnt think we shall be able to see the wheels of our Parliamentary machinery working in a perfectly satisfactory manner. The wants of the British community are great, and those who study the Parlia- mentary majority will have to cinsider in what way they may do justice to the claims and demands of Ire- land, and in what way they may do justice, on fair and equitable principles, to the claims and demands of Eng- land, Scotland, and Wales. (Hear, hear.) In your address from Blairgowrie, you have justly pointed out that our endeavour should bo to diminish a little of the misery that is in the world, to better the condition of out fellow subjects, to give them a more cheerful and happy lot in their pilgrimage through this earth, And thereby enable them, if so disposed, to pro- 'vide for their condition in another and More i durable existence. (Hear, hear.) One word more. In this election we were very sanguine. We have had some follies committed among ourselves. (Laughter, '"Perth.") There is the city of Perth, which 'ccustoined to regard with unmixed sada- ' for the moment got a little speck upon of its reputation, which I know it will mortunity in its power to redeem. (Hear, a.) Do not be discouraged because our ity in the House of Commons is not a very large one. It is between forty and fifty. If we had economised our resources at Perth and elsewhere might have been better. It will comfort you to know that I have sat in fifteen Parliaments and in five I have seen Liberal Governments in office, which have done a great deal of work for the country with not such a majority as is now returned to support Liberal principles. An- other point of considerable and curious interest. You know there is a body of gentimen ivho called themselves Liberal Unionists. (Laughter, and a voice "W. L. Reese.") It is very difficult for us —it is a very great stretch of courtesy for us to call them Littera! Unionists, because we do not think their conduct his tended to the union, but to the disunion of the coun- try. If I called them Liberal Unionists it is front my respect for them. They are gentlemen, who, I have not the slightest doubt, are in grievous error, and I do not doubt they have done what they thought it was their duty to do. It is my duty to believe it, and Ido believe it ; but I do not know whether you have observed it, gentlemen, that there has been a great change in their position in the last six years. They voted against us on Home Rule, and said "We must vote against you on everything else in order to keep in office a Government that is opposed to Home Rule." But look at the change. The Unionist votes in the last Parliament were given to support a Governmentopposed to Home Rule. Will they now continue giving Tory votes? I believe lam the first man that has put the question. (Hear, head.) ' As there are forty-five of them, it's a'question of some interest. I catyt help cherishing the hope that some of them will do right. lam certain many of them are honourable men, though I think they have been sadly misguided men ; but we shall be most curious to see what they will dO: We must hope for the best, although you often feel it is always wisest to expect the worst. (Laughter.) I look upon them with a kindly Interest; but whatever they do, whether they do their best or their worst, the Liberal cause does not depend upon them—(cheers)—and I trust Liberalism will be strong enough to set about the real prosecution cot its work with sincerity and earnest- ness and decision. (Hear, hear and cheers.) I with yod- el!, gentlemen and ladies, a most respectful farewell. I am very sensible of the kindness with which we have
r;Q • 1 ,cAr. ,
been received all along the route'. 1 feel it very deeply. I knew the heart of Scotland is a true heart. (Great cheering.)

Mrs. 'thadstor.e was then presented with a beautiful bouquet of roses, and Mr. Gladstone with a handsome hazel walking-stick with a ram's-horn handle. On the receipt of the latter, Mr. Gladstone caused consider- able amusement by asking—" Is this not like a stick for a bishop ?" (a Voice, " A leader," and laughter.) Hearty cheers were given as the party drove off after about a quarter of an hour's stay. The weather was clear, with brilliant sunshine, scarcely a cloud being overhead, and a pleasant northernly breeze prevailed, making the drive a very enjoyable one. ENTHUSIASTIC RECEPTION AT PITLOCHRY. Great interest was m inifested at Pitlochry in Mr. Gladstone's movements. By five o'clock people com- menced to congregate in the vicinity of Fisher's Hotel, and when the carriage appeared on the hill about six o'cicck many hundreds of both sexes, of all ages and of all shades of politics, had assembled. Nearly every occupant of the houses between Moulin and P "

turned out to obtain a glimpse of the ex-Premier, and when the carriage turned into the main street in Pitlochry loud and prolonged cheers were raised, and were kept up till the I entered the hotel. Mr. Gladstone, : 3nthusiasm of his adm:rers by bow After remainir in the hotel, Mr. Glad- stone came out at garden. He then took a short turn throui„ eoing up by the Estab- lished Church and the Bow. THE JOURNEY ON THURSDAY. Mr. Gladstone passed through Perth on Thursday on his way from Braemar. The right hon. gentleman stayed overnight at Pitlochry, which he left at two o'clock. On the platform at Perth were some thousands of people waiting the arrival of the train. Cheers were given, and Mrs Gladstone bowed, but he did not respond to calls for a speech. At Carlisle there was a large crowcit‘Co-cheered the right kon. gentleman, but no speech was made. At five minutes past twelve Mr. Gla4stone, Mrs. Glad- stone, Miss Helen Gladstone, and Mr. Armistead reached Chester General Railway Station. Having alighted, they were immediately driven to Flawarden Castle, which was reached shortly after one o'clock. The arrival was kept very quiet, but the few persons on the platform at Chester cheered Mr. Gladstone, who looked I well, but was no doubt fatigued by the long journey.

THOMAS COOPER, THE CHARTIST. The funeral of Thomas Cooper, the Chartist leadi and poet, who died yesterday week, took place at Lii coin, on Monday. The first part of the funeral servic was conducted in the Thomas Cooper Memorial Baptist Chapel, which was recently built and named in his honour. The service was conducted bv the Rev. Arthur O'Neill,of Birmingham,the Rev.E. H. Jackson,of Louth, and the Rev. J. Bennett. of Lincoln. After the service the Rev. Arthur O'Neill, a fellow Chartist prisoner, delivered an address. He said that it , was as nearly as possible fifty years since Thomas Cooper 4nd be stood together en a platform before 20,000 /people at Wednebbury. and he could well remember C.oper's ringing voice, the intense enthusiasm which he , felt, his deep sympathy and pity for the poor, his tre- mendous denunciation of wrong, and the fearless way in which he met oppressors. He rejoiced that after 50 years nearly every point they advocated had been accomplished. Mr. O'Neill went on to speak of the days he had spent in Stafford gaol in company with Cooper, ' and of a second occasion when he was in prison for a year with him. He commended to young men Cooper's' political and patriotic efforts as worthy of imitation. The Rev. E. H. Jackson also delivered an. address,'. and he was followed by the Rev. J. SHOCKING TRAGEDY. , • On Saturday evening, a man named Hackett, living at Waltliamstow, shot his wife and then killed himself. Hackett and his father-in-law were quarrelling, when Hackett drew a revolver and fired. His wife, unfortun- ately, ran between the men and received the shots. The man then turned the pistol on himself and fell dead instantly. The woman is not dead, but is not likely to recover.

On the 21st June, considerable excitement was occasioned in Earlestown and Newton by the circu- lation of a report that *kyoungwonian named mks Devereux:belonging to Newton, and engaged as held mistress at the St. John's Infant School, hed been assaulted whilst going home from school siting the Mesnes footpath. At that time the police objected to the publication of any particulars, as ely to hinder the course of justice, but it now appears the man who committed the assault has been ar- 'at Leigh. The facts briefly stated are that Miss eux was passing along the Mesnes towards New- ton, about five o'clock, on the 21st June, when a man, who was reclining on the grass, got up and followed her. He seized hold of Miss Devereux and threw her to the ground,placing his knee on her chest. She screamed, and an old man named Berry; having witnessed the assault, hurried to the spot, but the assailant made off towards Newton. !e .P.C. Cameron, whet happened to be close by, gave chase, but he was unable to overtake the ruffian, who got clear away. Later on in the evening he as- saulted a girl named Boardman, 13 years of age, on a footpath near her own home at Lowton, but in this case he wits also disturbed. The same day,about one o'clock, he committed a rape upon a girl 13 years of 'age, in the Mesnes field at Newton. The next day he assaulted two other girls at Leigh, and then after drawing £l3 from , the Savings Bank, betook himself to the Isle of Man. He returned from there a little over a week ago. On the Bth inst, he was arrested at Leigh on a charge of burglary, and was found to have some of the stolen c articles in his possession. He turned out to be a collier named George Eckersley, belonging to Leigh, and his description agreeing to some extent with that furnished by the Earlestown police, the latter were commuicated with'. The old man Berry, the girl Boardman, a shop- keeper named Pearson. and another girl were taken to Leigh, and they individually identified him from amongst six others, as the man wanted for the assaults at Newton. Miss Devereux, being away at the Isle of Man, has been unableto assist in the identification. The prisoner was brought up at Leigh on the various charges, and remanded until Thursday. The prisoner was brought up at Leigh Police Court. on Thursday morn- ,ing before Dr: Booth, charged with committing a rape upon Florence Vick, aged 13 at Newton, and also with attempting to assault Mary, Devereux, and Annie Boardman at Kenyon. Before the case was called Miss Devereux who has returned from the Isle of Man, readily identified her assailant from amongst a aumber of other men. It transpired from the evidence that the prisoner had spent the greater part of his life in prison and was ,only released in March last year, after blivirrgi served live years lor theft. Evidence having been giveit by a number of witnesses, the prisoner wbo had nothing to say, was ceimnitted to the Liverpool Assizes..•• . • • ,!.111111,

MARIAGE OF MISS A. P. BROWN TO
A NEW YORK EDITOR.

On Tuesday afternoon, the marriage of Miss .Aqelaide , Perrin , Brown, of Wilderspool-road, daughterfof the latelMr. Councillor John Brown, to her. cousin, Mr. Charles Rowland Brown, city editor of the New.iork Commercial Bulle- tin," and New York correspondent of the London "Financial News," was csklebrated at the Wesleyan Chapel, Bold-st., Warrington. The ceremony was pertormed by the Rev, Thomas Ross, in the presence of a pretty large congregation. The bride was given away by her brother Dr. W. P. Brown, Sower- by Bridge, Yorkshire, and the best 'mart was Mr. John Edwin Richardson, the bridesmaid e being Miss Emily Ainsworth Brown ttAd Miss Henrietta Brown, and Miss Mary Ann Ainsworth _Brown, the little" daughter or Dr. 'Brown. The bride was attired in a dress of French gray cloth, trimmed with gray. silk; arid a hat to mad, with white feathers, and she wore a broo4h of gold, diamonds, and pearls, the gift of the bridegroom. The two elder bridesmaids-wore navy blue dresses trimmed with silk,relieved with White lace, and large hats with white feathers.while the younger one was dressed in muslin delaine, and a iarge Leghorn hat to match. Master John Perrin Brown, son of Dr. Brown officiated As page, beirig clothed in sailor costume, the two children look- ing exceedingly pretty. The -organist played the wedding march at the close of the proceedings and the wedding breakfast was partaken of at the bride's home in Wilderspool-road, the bride and bridegroom as they entered the house being saluted with showers of rice. Among the guests were Mrs. Brown, wife of Dr. Brown, Mr. and Mrs. J. C. White, Mr. and Mrs. John Massey, and Mr. A. J. Brown. The bride and bridegroom proceeded dur- ing the afternoon to Llandudno, and will sail front Liverpool this (Saturday) afternoon for America. A BRAVE RESCUE AT STOCKTON • HEATH— ( „I • A boy was bravely rescued from 'drowning; at Stoekton Heath on Monday morning. The lad was grandson of Mrs. Wilkes and was playing, along with 1 other children, on the banks of the canal near LOn- don Bridge, when two of them fell into the water. The screams of the ehildre'n at once attracted the attention of Mr. Robert Isherwood who is in the employ of Mr. Robert Davie, and hem to the spot. Seeing what had occurred he threw off his coat and waistcoat and at once jumped into the water. he was just in time to save one -child, which was unconscious. and was not restored-to- animation for some time. This is, it is stated, the second- time Mr. Isherwood has displayed lits• courage in the saving of life. The other child was unfortunately drowned.—Mr.. Worsley, coroner, held an inquest at the Mulberry-Tree Inn, Stockton Heath, Warrington, on Wednesday morning, on the death of this boy, James Henry Burney, about nine years of age, on Mortdav morning. Mrs. Eliza Wilkes said her three grandchil- dren; deceased John Thomas, and Ada Burney, went to the canal to get a ball from their father which he pro- -mised-them the night before. The father's boat, how- ever, bad left early in the morning, and the children mugt have remained to play. Deceased, according to the evidence of thekrother,wasfloating,a piece of Ong tied to a string, When he-ifipped and fell in. and caught I hold of witness's leg and dragged him in also.—John ! Isherwood, gardener to Mr. Robert Davies, was ! working about 200 yards away,and hearing the screams ran to the spc,t. The canal is very deep, and Ilfteerr yards wide, but witness swam across and rescued Jr' Thomas Burney. Witness did not know much at restoring the apparently drowned, but he held the slightly upside down, and let the water run out Of mouth and nostrils. After seeing the lad breathe •st ness left him in charge of his friends and went and changed his clothes. Dr. Parker soon afterwards arrived, and completed the restoration of the boy, although it was two hours before be could spealc....lsher. wood said there was no sign whatever of the other boy being in the water, but as he was missed the canal was dragged, and the body found by a waterman named Yates. There was nobody about at the time of the occurrence. In answer to the coroner, Isherwood ' that eleven years ago he had effected a similar ‘t the same place, and had also saved a would-he- chi hauling him out with a boat hook.—The ronet, In summing up, referred in appropriate terms • Isherwood's bravery, and said he would lay the facts )efore the Royal Humane Society.—A verdict of "Found drowned" was returned.

THE ROYAL COURT THEATRE, WARRINGTON.
_ 1 sti

The building which has long been known as the Public Hall will be opened, on Thursday evening next, under its new title of "Royal Court Theatre." "Kindred Souls will be rendered on Thursday, Fri- day, and Saturday evenings, Friday being the grand fashionable night. Mr. Arthur Milton will appear as Frank Frith, Mr. Percy Milton as Flutterwig, and they will be supported by the Milton Rays Comedy Company. A few weeks ago we gave an account of the alterations that were projected in order to make the Hall more suitable for its new uses, and these alterations are now well on towards corn pletion, though there are still many workmen busily engaged on the work. The alterations are being carried out by Mr. John Bland, contractor, ot Manchester, to the designs of Messrs. Darbyshire c and Smith, architects, Manchester. Though the hall is still far from having put on its finished ap- pearance, a general idea may be got of the main alterations. The gallery, for instance, has been brought forward considerably and therefore en- larged, and at each side of the stage there a private box has been constructed. The stage, too, has been lowered, and, the organ having been removed, it has been much extended by being carried back to the side wall of the building. Several desirable improvements have also been carried out in regard to dressing-rooms, &c. The hall is being handsomely decorated, and, in fact,every effort is being made to make it, as a theatre, a credit to the town. .

THE LIVERPOOL WIFE MURDER., THE ACCUSED BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

On Wednesday, William Williamson, aged 68, was ! brought up before Mr. Philip Rathbone and Dr. Marsh on the charge of having wilfully murdered his wife, on ' Tuesday, at their lodgings, 19, Beresford-st., Livtrpool. The prislner is a frail,slightly-built man, of low stature, with thin grey hair, and as he stood in the dock he be- trayed evident signs of the anxiety under which he laboured. He was not professionally assisted. Mr. Moss, who appeared for the prosecution, said : The prisoner, William Williamson, is chaiged with hav- ing, on Tuesday afternoon, murdered his wife, by cut- ting her throat with a razor. I shall only give you suffi- dent evidence to enable you to remand the prisoner until Monday next, when I hope to be in a position to get the case advanced to send him to the Assizes. William Hay (P.O. 31E) deposed : On Tuesday after- noon I was called to the house, 19,Beresford-st., when I saw the prisoner. I charged him with the murder of his wife, and, in answer to the charge, he said, " I done it." "

The prisoner was then remanded until Monday next. On Thursday an inquest was held by the Liverpool coroner. Evidence was given by several witnesses as to the aggravatina conduct of the deceased, and the jury returned a verdict of wilful murder against Wit- , liamson ; but under circumstances of very great provo- cation. . _

The annual meeting of the Grand Lode of the Orange Institution of England was opened at Southport, on Wednesday, under the presidency of Brother Robert Todd, of London, Deputy Grand Master. The business, was mainly of a routine character.

THE STORK -WRECK AND LOSS OF LIFE NEAR LIVERPOOL. The storm on Tuesday night resulted in lamentable loss of life near Liverpool. The Liverpool lifeboat went out in tow of a tug to the assistance of a vessel which had gone ashore near the Mersey bar. By great efforts the lifeboat crew got their craft alongside the stranded ;hip, and then she was struck by a heavy cross sea and turned over, the men, 13 in number, being thrown into the water. Two were drowned, but the remainder, three of whom were badly Injured, managed to get back to the boat, which drifted abont for several hours, going ashore at length near Leasowe. After their long exposure to cold and the buffeting of terrific seas, the survivors were of course in a very exhausted state. They, however, managed to land, and the injured were taken to Hoylake Cottage Hospital, where one of them soon afterwards died. The ship to which the lifeboat was summoned was the Maxwell, which left Birken- head for San Francisco on Tuesday afternoon. ' Her crew was rescued by the New Brightoh lifeboat. News has been received of the loss of two fishing vessels —one off Whitby and the other at Sark—during the torm. In each of these cases three men were drowned. The Glasgow collier Elfrida, which went ashore in the Medway, has been floated.

div.head: A, LEVEL CROSSING ACCIDENT.
div.p: A, LEVEL CROSSING ACCIDENT.

• A Midland express train dashed into a hay cart at the level crossing near New Mills, twelve miles from Man- chester, on Thursday night. A youth on the cart was thrown twenty-five yards, and sustained a broken arm and a scalp wound.

div.head: PRECAUTIONS AGAINST CHOLERA.
div.p: PRECAUTIONS AGAINST CHOLERA.

The Scottish Board of Supervision, with a view of preventing the importation of chotera, has directed the port authorities to prohilait the landing of rags from France, Russia Roumania, Bulgaria, Turkey, Sea of Azoff, and Black Sea. THE PLAGUE IN RUSSIA. DECREASED MORTALITY. Sr. PETERSBURG, FRlDAY.—According to the latest figures cholera is increasing in Saratoff, and the death rate is higher at Samara, though there is a falling off in the number of cases at the latter place. The mortality shows a further decrease in Astrachan, where there were 198 cases and 57 deaths on the 19th, as compared with 195 cases and 132 deaths on the previous day. At Samara 58 zases and 43 deaths occurred, against 75 on the preceding day.

THE RISLEY MEETING. Shooting in the " Graphic" competition concluded yesterday morning, arid the winner of the cup, which is valued at 50 guineas, is Sergeant Sheldon, of the Royal Engineers, who made an aggregate of 68, viz., 35 at 200 yards and 33 at 500 yards. Sergeant Colman, 4th Liver- pool, and Private Geddes, Bth Lanark, came next, with 67.

TUE NATIONALISTS AND THE *.RISFUNDS. Paws, FRlDAY.—Yesterday in tbe Civil Court of the Seine, the cause M'Carthy versus Munroe and Co., bankers, Mrs. Parnell, Dr. Keany, and Mr. Harrington was called on. As is well known, it refers to a dispute as to who should have possession of the million francs entrusted to the first named, and which are the balance af the American subscriptions on behalf of the Irish party. Mr. M'Carthy claims, as head of the Irish Nationalist party, to be entitled to the money, and he therefore asks for an order for it to be delivered to him with costs against the defendants. After hearing corn, arguments the case was remanded for a week: • • AN ASYLUM DESTROYED. REPORTED GREAT LOSS OF LIFE. NEW YORK, FRIDAY.—A despatch has been received here from La Paz Bolivia announcing the destruction by fire of the orphan asylum there. It states that all the men and children in toe institution lost their lives.

div.head: WESLEYAN CONFERENCE.
div.p: WESLEYAN CONFERENCE.

At the Wesleyan Conference at Bradford yesterday morning, consideration was given to the applications for the transfer of ministers from other conferences. The Rev. F. R. DOM, of Newfoundland, was accepted. A proposal of the Rev. H. P. Hughes to copyright the stations of ministers was not accepted. It was agreed that in future thereshould be a public session to include the President's address on the opening day of the Con- ference. SETTLEMENT OF A STRIKE AT BOLroN.

The strike of plumbers and glaziers at Bolton, which has extended over twelve week* and brought about a general lock-out in the building trade there, was settled yesterday by arbitration, and work will be resumed on Monday. The trouble arose over rules relating to time of starting in winter and out of, town ,allowanoe. The umpire's award places the men on the same footing as those in Manchester and other large towns. _ , _
ANOTHER AN.O.IICtIIST PLOT.

NUMEROUS 'ARRESTS IN PARIS. Peals, THllRSDAY.—According to this morning's " Figaro "the police are said to have discovered another Anarchist plot, the object of which was to take concerted and simultaneous action ..f.:tr the blowing up of the Bourse, the Palais Iburbon, and P.alais de Justice. It is sated that four deserters from the French army,who were living abroad, were chosen to carry out the Anarchist plans, and that two of them who recently arrived in Parks wers carrested on Wednesday. A gang of 26 male- factbrs alto 'fell into the hands of the police on Wednes- day. They all profess Anarchis;; doctrines.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. WILLIAM REID.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. WILLIAM REID.

The death of Mr. Wm. Reid, a well-known resi- dent of Warrington, took place on Saturday mor, ing. On the Tuesday previous he took ill ratl suddenly, and though he rallied again to some tent he passed away as stated on Saturday. Mr. Reid was for close upon 30 years in the employ of Messrs. Peter Walker and Son, for a considerable time as manager. He retired from this service in 1889, and wq,s presented by the other employes and officials with a silver salver and tea and coffee ser- vice. The salver bore the following inscription : "This salver, together with tea and coffee servir was presented with best wishes to William T' Esq., by the employes of Messrs. Peter Walke

Soli,' on his rdire-ment from the management of the business, after 29 years' service." After being released from the ties of business, Mr. Reid, accom- panied by Mr. F. Massey, paid a visit to New Zea- land, by which he benefited much in health. The deceased was 60 years of age, and leaves a widow and family. The funeral took place on Tuesday afternoon, at St. Paul's Church, in the midst of a heavy downpour of rain. The R.N. 11. V. Pigot, vicar, officiated, and in the drenching rain the second poition of the service was gone through in the churchyard in the presence of a fairly large num- ber of friends. The mournsrs were Mr. C. P. Reid, Mr. W. A. Reid, (sons) ; Mr. Isaac, Mr. William R. Arthur, Mr: John B. Arthur, and Mr. Frederic Arthur (nephews) ; Messrs. W. H. Walker, T. H. Pilkington, J. -- PICNICS.—A number of picnic Parties visited the village on Saturday, Sunday, and Monday. The annual straw- berry fair was continued on Sunday, when there Wel again a good attendance. The demand for eberneS• strawberries, and flowers was good, and fair prices were realized, though the quantity was limited. Cwoin TRIP.—Tbe choir, Sunday school teachers, add members of the congregation and friends of Christ • Church, Croft, had their annual trip OR Saturday, the place selected being Llandudno. The party left at 7-30 and arrived at Llandudno at half-past ten. Rain fell heavily until about noon. The party, however, under the direction of Mr. Cawthorn, organist and choir master, made the best of the circumstances, and visited the principal places of inlerest. The afternoon and even- • ing were fine, which added much to their enjoyment, and they left Llandudno by the 6.40 p.m. train, and arrived safely at Kenyon Junction about 10.30. RETIREMENT OF THE RECTOII.—The Rev. TP. man, M.A., F.R.S., rector, has now left the parish,after spending upwards of 53 years in the ministry. " Per: haps very few, if any, ministers of the Church.ox England possessing such noble talents have been se buried (says a well known Congregation:ost writer) in such an out-of-way or rural pleasant place as Croft,when he might probably have been promoted to a much . higher position." However, so it is. Coming tw• the- . Kirk- parish from Lymm, where he held a curacy at the Parish Church until 1839, and, sacceeding the first in- cumbent of Croft, the Rev. Mr. Banning, he became the rector of the parish, when it was carved out of the old parish of Virinwibk by the Winwick Rectory Act, and. thus he has laboured eonthauallv, with the exception or a few well-earned holidays each. year, until now. The Rector did not preach a farewell sermon, but he alluded both morning and afternoon to the condition of the parish, to the welfare of the members of the congrega- tion, and to their attendance at church. There was a large congregation at each service.
